242: Common Questions
243: Quick answers to help you get started.
244: What is the HubSpot Developer Platform?
245: The HubSpot Developer Platform is a unified foundation that empowers you to build and deliver value faster — one way to build on HubSpot, from private integrations to Marketplace apps. It includes the CLI, projects framework, UI extensions, and APIs plus an AI‑ready framework and capabilities like Breeze Agent Tools.
246: What are Projects?
247: Projects are the unified framework for building apps (and CMS assets) on the HubSpot Developer Platform: unified projects that can support one account or many. A project is a collection of code, configuration, and assets managed through the CLI with date-based versioning (like 2026.03).
248: When are new platform versions and APIs released?
249: Both follow the same 6-month release cycle: March and September. Each platform version is supported for 18 months, giving you ample time to plan upgrades. API versioning is independent meaning you can use newer APIs on older platform versions.
250: Check the changelog for release announcements and deprecation notices. Subscribe for updates
251: Do I need a paid HubSpot account to develop?
252: No. You can create a free HubSpot account and build apps without a paid subscription. You'll get access to a developer test account with sample data for testing. For production deployments, your app's users will need appropriate HubSpot accounts.
253: What does a developer account come with?
254: A free developer account includes:
255: Test accounts with sample CRM data (contacts, companies, deals) for development and testing
256: API access to HubSpot’s public APIs for development and testing
257: App management to create, configure, and publish apps
258: CLI access to create and deploy Projects
259: AI-native developer documentation
260: Test accounts reset periodically but are fully functional for building and testing your integrations.
261: What are developer seats?
262: When you convert your developer portal, you get 2 Super Admin core seats with full access to CRM and development tools. Additional users can be added as developer seats which provide access to development tools without using a paid CRM seat.
263: Developer seats let your team collaborate on apps without requiring paid HubSpot subscriptions.
264: Learn more about account types
265: What languages and frameworks are supported?
266: UI Extensions: React (TypeScript or JavaScript)
267: Backend integrations: Any language that can make HTTP requests; HubSpot's APIs are RESTful
268: CLI tooling: Node.js
269: Serverless functions: Node.js (currently supported on Projects 2025.1; see docs for the latest roadmap and migration guidance)
270: AI tooling: MCP server support for IDE copilots (Cursor, Claude Code, VS Code, Windsurf)
271: How do I know which platform version I'm on?
272: Check the platformVersion field in your hsproject.json file. Apps on version 2025.2 or later are on the current platform.
273: If you're on an earlier version, see the "I have an existing app" path above to upgrade to the latest Projects framework.
274: Note: Version numbers are date-based. Use 2026.03 (March), not 2026.3.
275: Why should I migrate my existing app? When is the best time?
276: The new platform offers better performance, modern UI Extensions (app cards, App Home, settings pages), improved developer tooling, and ongoing feature updates including AI capabilities.
277: Legacy apps on older versions will be deprecated over time. Projects 2025.1 deprecates June 1, 2026. Migrating ensures your app stays supported and can take advantage of new capabilities.
278: See the migration timeline
279: What’s the difference between portal conversion and app migration?
280: They're separate steps: Portal conversion updates your developer portal itself — converting it from the legacy Developer Tools view to a HubSpot Free CRM account with the Development navigation. This is a one-time step that must be completed before you can migrate apps.
281: App migration moves individual apps to the new Projects framework (2025.2 or later). Each app migrates separately using CLI commands. If your portal is already on the new platform (you see "Development" in the nav), you can skip portal conversion and go straight to app migration.
282: What does “migration” mean for my app?
283: Migration moves your app to the new Projects framework. What's involved depends on where you're starting:
284: Legacy public apps use OAuth and can be installed in multiple portals; they may or may not be listed in the Marketplace.
285: Legacy private apps use API keys and work only in a single portal.
286: This distinction affects your migration path and install limits. If you’re still using a legacy developer portal, you’ll convert that portal to the new Developer Platform through the in‑app opt‑in banner then move individual apps using the migration guides.
287: See the migration matrix guide
288: Do I need to migrate from legacy CRM cards to app cards?
289: Yes, Classic CRM cards sunset on October 31, 2026. App cards are the replacement — they're built with React, support richer interaction and work across more surfaces (record pages, App Home, settings).
290: If you're migrating an app that uses classic CRM cards, you'll need to rebuild them as app cards.
291: Classic CRM cards sunset details
292: Create an app card
293: What’s the status of serverless functions?
294: Serverless functions are currently supported only in Projects 2025.1. They're not yet available on 2025.2 or later.
295: What this means for you: New apps should build without serverless for now or start on 2025.1 and migrate later. Existing apps using serverless should stay on 2025.1 until 2026.03 (March 2026).
296: We'll share updates on 2026.03 serverless support in the changelog.
297: Read serverless migration strategies
298: Should I migrate or start fresh?
299: If you're already on Projects 2025.1 with app cards → migration to 2025.2 or later is lightweight.
300: If you're on a legacy app with significant tech debt → starting fresh might be faster.
301: Run hs project migrate to see what's involved.

76: Authentication
77: Authentication overview
78: Learn how to manage authentication for your apps and when developing locally.
79: While building apps on the developer platform, you can configure authentication based on how you plan to install your app. HubSpot also provides local authentication tooling via the HubSpot CLI.
80: App authentication
81: There are two authentication types available based on how you plan to distribute your app: OAuth is required for multiple accounts, while static auth access tokens are used for installing in a single account at a time.
82: OAuth
83: If you plan to distribute your app to multiple accounts (either through listing on the HubSpot Marketplace or by managing specific authorized accounts), your app must be built using OAuth authentication. You’ll need to set up and host an OAuth backend service (e.g., hosted as a Docker instance using a cloud service provider) to initiate the OAuth process and manage token data for users installing your app in their account.
84: HubSpot provides a Node.js quickstart guide here, which includes code you can run in a Docker instance with full OAuth support. Authentication configuration details for your app are available on the app details page in the developer overview of your HubSpot account.
85: Once you’ve set up an OAuth backend, you can make API requests using the OAuth access token that corresponds to a user who installed your app. This access token is provided using the Bearer HTTP authorization header. For example, if you wanted to retrieve contacts for the account with an access token of 00000000-aaaa-xxx-yyyy-zzzzzzzzzzzz, your request would resemble the following:
86: curl --request GET \
87: --header "Authorization: Bearer 00000000-aaaa-xxx-yyyy-zzzzzzzzzzzz" \
88: --url "https://api.hubapi.com/crm/objects/2026-03/contacts?limit=10&archived=false"
89: Configure your app to use OAuth by setting the type subproperty within the auth field of your app’s app-hsmeta.json config to oauth. You’ll also need to set the distribution property to marketplace or private based on how you plan to distribute your app:
90: marketplace: used if you want the app to be eligible for listing on the HubSpot Marketplace.
91: private: used if you only want to install your app in a specific set of allowlisted accounts. If you choose this option, you can install your app in a maximum of 10 accounts at a time.
92: Learn more in the app configuration guide.
93: Static auth
94: If you want to limit distribution of your app to a single authorized account, you’ll use a static auth access token. This token can be found in your app settings. An example request is provided below using a placeholder static auth access token.
95: curl --request GET \
96: --header "Authorization: Bearer ***-***-*********-****-****-****-************" \
97: --url "https://api.hubapi.com/crm/objects/2026-03/contacts?limit=10&archived=false"
98: Configure your app to use static auth by setting the type subproperty (within the auth field) in your app’s app-hsmeta.json config to static, and set the distribution field to private.
99: Learn more in the app configuration guide.
100: Developer API keys
101: Some app features and settings require a developer API key, which is available in the developer overview of your HubSpot account.
102: If a feature or endpoint requires a developer API key, it’ll be documented in the associated guide or reference article. You’ll provide the key value in the hapikey query parameter, usually with the appId query parameter which corresponds to the app you’re making changes to. For example, the cURL snippet below provides an example of using the custom channel registration endpoint:
103: curl --request POST \
104: --url "https://api.hubapi.com/conversations/custom-channels/2026-03?hapikey={YOUR_DEVELOPER_API_KEY}&appId={appId}"
105: Client credentials
106: Similar to HubSpot developer API keys, HubSpot uses client credential tokens to take an action on behalf of your app. These tokens are OAuth 2.0 tokens with short-term expiry windows that must be refreshed after a certain amount of time.
107: Unlike the OAuth tokens used for app authentication, client credential tokens aren’t used to act on behalf of users who install your app. Instead, they’re used to manage your app’s global configuration for specific features.
108: Currently, the only feature using client credential tokens is the webhooks journal API. For example, to generate a client credentials token with all available webhook journal and management permissions, you’d make the following API call:
109: curl --location 'https://api.hubapi.com/oauth/2026-03/token' \
110: --header 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
111: --data-urlencode 'grant_type=client_credentials' \
112: --data-urlencode 'client_id=XXXXXXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX' \
113: --data-urlencode 'client_secret=XXXXXXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX' \
114: --data-urlencode 'scope=developer.webhooks_journal.read developer.webhooks_journal.subscriptions.read developer.webhooks_journal.subscriptions.write developer.webhooks_journal.snapshots.read developer.webhooks_journal.snapshots.write'
115: Scopes
116: Based on the HubSpot data and functionality that your app will require access to, you’ll provide a list of scopes in your app’s app-hsmeta.json authentication config. For example, if your app required access to create contacts, you’d need to include the crm.objects.contacts.write.
117: Learn more about scopes.
118: Local authentication
119: While you develop your app locally using the HubSpot CLI, you can use the hs accounts auth command. If you’re configuring local authentication for the first time, you can also use the hs init command. After authenticating, a personal access key will be associated with your account that will be used to authenticate CLI commands.
120: Learn more about installing the HubSpot CLI. A full list of CLI commands is provided here.
121: Client secret rotation
122: A client secret is a confidential value specific to your app, which is used for managing OAuth tokens, validating requests from HubSpot, and generating a client credentials token.
123: If this secret is compromised (e.g., you mistakenly committed the secret to a git repository), you can rotate the secret to ensure the old one is invalidated and cannot be used.
124: Client secret rotation is supported for legacy public apps, project-based apps on the developer platform, and MCP auth apps.
125: Learn how to rotate a client secret in a project-based app.

53: Legacy private apps
54: Learn how to manage legacy private apps in HubSpot.
55: As of October 26, 2026, legacy private apps can no longer be created. Learn more about this sunset on the HubSpot Developer Changelog
56: Existing legacy apps are still supported by HubSpot, but don't have access to the latest app features. Learn more about the new developer platform.
57: To access legacy apps in your standard HubSpot account, navigate to Development, then click Legacy apps in the left sidebar menu.
58: Private apps allow you to use HubSpot’s APIs to access specific data from your HubSpot account. You can authorize what each private app can request or change in your account, which will generate an access token that’s unique to your app.
59: You must be a super admin to access private apps in your HubSpot account.
60: Feature limitations
61: Webhooks are supported in private apps, but subscriptions cannot be edited programmatically via an API, and must instead be edited in your private app settings.
62: Private apps do not support custom timeline events, if you plan on building an app using custom timeline events, you should create a public app instead. Learn more about the differences between private and public apps.
63: Make API calls with your app’s access token
64: To start making API calls, navigate to the details page of your app.
65: In your HubSpot account, navigate to Development.
66: In the left sidebar menu, navigate to Legacy apps.
67: Click the name of your app.
68: Click the Auth tab, click Show token to reveal your access token. Click Copy to copy the token to your clipboard.
69: You can then paste the access token to provide it to your developers, or use it yourself as you develop your app. When making a call to one of the HubSpot API endpoints, set the value of the Authorization field to Bearer [YOUR_TOKEN]. For example, if you’re making a call to the Contacts API using Node.js and axios, the request would look like the following:
70: axios.get(
71: "https://api.hubapi.com/crm/v3/objects/contacts",
72: {
73: headers: {
74: Authorization: `Bearer ${YOUR_TOKEN}`,
75: "Content-Type": "application/json",
76: },
77: },
78: (err, data) => {
79: // Handle the API response
80: }
81: );
82: Private app access tokens are implemented on top of OAuth, so you can also make authenticated calls with your access token using one of HubSpot’s client libraries. For example, if you’re using the Node.js client library, you can instantiate an OAuth client by passing in your app’s access token:
83: const hubspotClient = new hubspot.Client({ accessToken: YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN });
84: Access tokens may be restricted or intentionally fail in the following cases:
85: Private apps will lose access to scopes when your HubSpot account is downgraded and loses access to functionality.
86: For example, if your account does not have access to HubDB, your private app will not have access to the HubDB scope.
87: Private app access tokens will be updated to reflect available scopes in your HubSpot account and what you configured for the private app, but the token string itself will not change.
88: If you remove the user who originally created a private app, some API calls that previously used the app’s access token will fail with a result of "USER_DOES_NOT_HAVE_PERMISSIONS".
89: If this issue occurs, it’s recommended that you follow the instructions in the section below to rotate your access token.
90: If you mistakenly removed the user from your account, adding them back will also fix the issue.
91: View private app access token information
92: To view information about a private app’s access token, such as the Hub ID and scopes associated with the token, make a POST request to /oauth/v2/private-apps/get/access-token-info. In the request body, include your access token:
93: {
94: "tokenKey": YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN
95: }
96: The response will include information about the user who created the token, the Hub ID of the account, the private app ID, and the scopes associated with the token.
97: {
98: "userId": 123456,
99: "hubId": 1020304,
100: "appId": 2011410,
101: "scopes": ["crm.schemas.companies.write"]
102: }
103: Rotate your access token
104: If your access token is lost or otherwise compromised, you can rotate the token. A new access token will be created and the original access token will expire.
105: In your HubSpot account, navigate to Development.
106: In the left sidebar menu, navigate to Legacy apps.
107: Click the name of your private app.
108: Next to your access token, click Rotate:
109: If your token is compromised and you want to immediately revoke access, click Rotate and expire now.
110: If there’s no imminent threat to your token, it’s still recommended that you rotate your token every six months. If you’re ready to initiate a regular rotation of your token, click Rotate and expire later, which will trigger an expiration of the token in 7 days.
111: If your app is ready to transition earlier, you can click Expire now.
112: If you decide you need more time, you can click Cancel rotation, which will cancel the expiration of the original token and revoke the new access token.
113: HubSpot will also send email notifications to super admins with reminders about access token rotation status, as well as other related alerts. Super admins in your HubSpot account will receive notifications for the following events and reminders:
114: A super admin initiated a rotation (either immediately or scheduled for 7 days from now).
115: A super admin canceled a pending rotation.
116: A super admin opted to expire an access token immediately by clicking Expire now instead of waiting 7 days for the token to expire.
117: The app’s access token is about to expire in 24 hours.
118: The app’s access token has been rotated and expired after 7 days.
119: If you haven’t rotated your access token in over 180 days, super admins will also receive a reminder email to rotate your app’s access token.
120: View API call logs
121: To review the API calls your app has made in the past 30 days:
122: On the details page of your app, click the Logs tab.
123: Review and filter your private app API calls:
124: Click the Method and Response dropdown menus to filter your historical API calls by request method or response code.
125: Click the start date or end date dropdown menus to narrow your call logs to a specific time range.
126: You can also search for specific calls by URL in the Search by request URL search box.
127: Please note: HubSpot does not store the request body, request URL parameters, or response payload of successful API calls in the logs for private apps. If you want to track this data, or you want to store log data from more than 30 days ago, it’s recommended that you maintain an external log of your app’s historical calls.
128: To export the API call logs, click Export logs (CSV). Then, specify a date range (up to the past 30 days) and click Export.
129: In the pop-up box, select the date range of API calls you want to export and click Export. You will receive an email with a download link when the export is ready.
130: Private app limits
131: You can create up to 20 private apps in your HubSpot account. Each private app is subject to HubSpot’s API usage guidelines. The number of calls your private app can make is based on your account subscription and whether you’ve purchased the API add-on:
132: Product TierPer 10 SecondsPer Day
133: Private Apps(Any Hub)Free and Starter100 / private app250,000 / account
134: (Any Hub)Professional190 / private app625,000 / account
135: (Any Hub)Enterprise190 / private app1,000,000 / account
136: Private Apps with API Limit Increase(Any Hub)Free, Starter, Professional, and Enterprise200 / private app1,000,000 / account on top of your base subscription, for each limit increase. You can purchase a maximum of two API limit increase.
137: If you have both a Starter and Professional plan, limits for the higher tier (Professional) apply to your account.
138: You can make a GET request to /account-info/v3/api-usage/daily/private-apps to review the daily API usage for all private apps in your HubSpot account. Learn more about using the account information API.
139: Please note:Purchasing an API Limit Increase will increase the maximum number of requests you can make to the associations API to 1,000,000 daily requests and 200 requests per 10 seconds, but these limits cannot be increased further with an additional API Limit Increase purchase.
140: Delete a private app
141: When you delete one of your private apps, its access token will be permanently revoked and you’ll no longer be able to use it to make API calls.
142: To delete an app:
143: In your HubSpot account, navigate to Development.
144: In the left sidebar menu, navigate to Legacy apps.
145: Click the name of your private app.
146: At the top of the page, click the Auth tab.
147: At the bottom of the page, click Delete [name of your app].
148: In the dialog box, type the name of your app to confirm its deletion, then click Delete.

119: Reference documentation for HubSpot’s 2026-09 APIs
120: The 2026-09 APIs use a date-based versioning scheme (e.g., /crm/2026-09/) that follows the previous 2026-03 API version. All endpoints in this section follow the pattern:
121: /api-name/2026-09/resource
122: For example, to retrieve all contacts:
123: GET /crm/objects/2026-09/contacts
124: All APIs, whether legacy, new, or beta, use the same root path as before: https://api.hubapi.com/.
125: This versioning model gives HubSpot the ability to ship updates on a predictable schedule. When a new date version is released, the previous version continues to work until its end-of-life date, giving you time to migrate. For new integrations, always use the latest date version. Learn more about this change on HubSpot’s Developer Changelog.
126: Across the API reference section, use the versioning dropdown menu in the top bar to switch versions. If there’s an equivalent endpoint to the one you’re currently viewing, you’ll automatically be sent there. Otherwise, you’ll land on that version’s home page.

75: Integrate AI tools with the HubSpot MCP server
76: Learn how to configure a connector to authenticate requests to the HubSpot MCP server for interacting with HubSpot’s APIs.
77: The HubSpot Model Context Protocol (MCP) server enables AI assistants and Large Language Models to securely interact with your HubSpot CRM data through natural conversation. By implementing the Model Context Protocol standard, this remote server acts as a bridge between AI systems and HubSpot’s APIs, allowing for intelligent automation and insights without requiring users to understand complex API structures.
78: For developers, the remote HubSpot MCP server provides secure, granular access to HubSpot CRM data through AI agents and third-party applications, and allows teams to build custom workflows, automate reporting, and integrate HubSpot context into third-party applications. For end-users, it creates a more streamlined, simpler way to query their HubSpot data using natural language.
79: For guidance on when to use the HubSpot MCP server, check out recommended use cases.
80: The HubSpot MCP server documented on this page is separate from the developer MCP server. The developer MCP server helps developers build apps and CMS content assets locally on HubSpot’s developer platform. In contrast, the HubSpot MCP server is intended for making requests to an account’s CRM data, similar to using HubSpot’s APIs.
81: Implementation overview
82: At a high level, integrating with the HubSpot MCP server involves:
83: Creating an MCP connector in your HubSpot account.
84: Configuring your MCP client to connect to the HubSpot MCP server at https://mcp.hubspot.com using your connector’s OAuth credentials.
85: Prompting your MCP client using natural language to query your HubSpot data.
86: Once you’ve created your MCP connector, you can use it with any MCP client that supports OAuth authentication with PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange). PKCE is required for authenticating with HubSpot’s MCP server.
87: Some MCP clients, like the MCP Inspector, handle PKCE automatically. If you’re building a custom integration, ensure your OAuth implementation includes PKCE support. Learn more about OAuth 2.1 authorization in the MCP specification.
88: Supported data and permissions
89: The following data is accessible via the remote MCP server.
90: Please note: if your HubSpot account has Sensitive Data turned on, conversation data will be blocked from access through the MCP server. This restriction is specific to the MCP server and does not apply to the standard CRM APIs.
91: Read access
92: CRM records: contacts, companies, deals, tickets, leads, users, appointments, courses, listings, projects, services, custom objects, and segments (lists). Revenue objects (carts, invoices, orders, line items, products, quotes, subscriptions) are available in BETA.
93: Activities: calls, emails, meetings, notes, and tasks.
94: Content and marketing: blog posts, landing pages, site pages, campaigns, and marketing events.
95: Content analytics: conversion rates, submissions, and views for landing pages, website pages, and blog posts.
96: Communication content: search the content of call and meeting transcripts, email bodies, notes, meetings, inbox conversations, knowledge base articles, and files.
97: Conversations: messages and threads from live chat, team email, WhatsApp, SMS, Facebook Messenger, and custom channels connected to help desk or conversations inbox.
98: Conversations access has additional restrictions based on your HubSpot inbox configuration.
99: Help desk conversations are visible to all users.
100: For the conversations inbox, if access has been restricted to specific users or teams, only those users can query those conversations through the MCP server.
101: Marketing emails: draft emails and previews, email analytics data including aggregate send statistics (sends, opens, clicks, bounces, unsubscribes, and deliveries), account email health diagnostics, and per-contact delivery and engagement details.
102: Social: list your connected social accounts, browse scheduled and published posts, and view post performance data.
103: User and account: authenticated user details and permissions, account information, and organization-wide data including teams, job titles, seat counts, and brands.
104: AEO: brand-level metrics, share of voice, tracked prompt performance, and full AI engine response text from ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Claude. Available in HubSpot accounts with a Marketing Hub Professional or Enterprise subscription.
105: Behind the scenes, the HubSpot MCP server is based on the CRM search API, which currently doesn’t include vector search capabilities.
106: Write access
107: CRM records: create and edit contacts, companies, deals, tickets, leads, line items, products, appointments, courses, listings, projects, services, and custom object records. When creating or updating CRM records, the MCP server respects conditional field logic including custom pipeline stage validations.
108: Activities: calls, emails, meetings, notes, and tasks.
109: Content: create, edit, and publish landing pages, website pages, and blog posts.
110: Campaigns: create and update campaigns and manage campaign asset associations.
111: Marketing emails: create and update email drafts.
112: Pipelines: create and manage pipelines for supported objects. For HubSpot accounts with free tools, creating custom pipelines is not supported, but this tool can edit the default HubSpot-provided pipeline.
113: Properties: create custom properties for CRM objects.
114: Quotes (BETA): create and manage quotes. Requires the manage revenue objects optional scope and is available in HubSpot accounts with a Revenue Hub Professional or Enterprise subscription.
115: Segments: create static segments and add or remove records from existing segments.
116: AEO: create tracked prompts and act on brand recommendations, including starting content generation actions such as blog posts and social posts. Available in HubSpot accounts with a Marketing Hub Professional or Enterprise subscription.
117: Social: create drafts, schedule posts, update or cancel scheduled posts, upload local media, preview posts before publishing, and assign posts to campaigns.
118: To create or modify social posts through the MCP server, you must grant the social.publish scope. The social.read and social.edit scopes only provide read-only access.
119: Permissions and scopes
120: All actions respect your existing HubSpot user permissions. Users can only view and modify records they have access to in HubSpot.
121: When creating an MCP connector, it’s important to note that you don’t explicitly define the connector’s scopes. Instead, available scopes are automatically determined by two factors:
122: The tools available in the MCP server at the time of installation.
123: The permissions that the user chooses to grant during installation.
124: As the MCP server’s tools are updated, the available scopes may change. In the event of scope updates, users who have already installed the connector will need to re-install to grant any new scopes.
125: Claude Enterprise admins can restrict connector access to company-provisioned accounts only by enabling verified domain restrictions in their account settings.
126: Available tools
127: Tool availability varies by HubSpot subscription, user permissions, and account configuration. Run get_user_details after connecting to check which tools and objects are available for your specific account. The list below covers publicly available tools; some MCP clients may offer additional provider-specific tools not listed here.
128: Create an MCP connector
129: Create an MCP connector in your HubSpot account.
130: In the main navigation bar of your HubSpot account, navigate to Development.
131: In the left sidebar menu, navigate to MCP Connectors.
132: In the upper right, click Create MCP connector.
133: In the dialog box, enter your connector details, which you can update later as needed:
134: Name: the name of your connector.
135: Description: an optional description of your connector.
136: Redirect URL: the URL to use for OAuth authentication. If you’ll be testing with the MCP inspector, you’ll need to include http://localhost:6274/oauth/callback/debug as a redirect URL.
137: Icon: an optional icon for your connector.
138: Click Create.
139: HubSpot will then generate a connector configured with OAuth authentication using the details you provided. You’ll then be redirected to the connector’s details page, where you can view its client credentials, redirect URLs, and more. To edit your connector details, you can click Edit info in the upper right.
140: If you’re including multiple redirect URLs, the first redirect URL will be used as the default redirect.
141: You can then proceed to connect your MCP client to the HubSpot MCP server, using your connector to authenticate requests.
142: For quick testing, you can use the MCP inspector tool, as described in the next section. Otherwise, you can continue to the General MCP client connection section for general instructions.
143: Test with the MCP inspector
144: The MCP Inspector is a debugging tool that handles OAuth with PKCE automatically, making it a quick way to test your connection to HubSpot’s MCP server without building a full integration.
145: The MCP Inspector is a third-party tool maintained by the MCP community. Consult the MCP Inspector documentation for the most up-to-date setup instructions, as its interface is subject to change.
146: To connect using MCP Inspector:
147: Run the MCP Inspector tool locally.
148: Configure the connection using the Streamable HTTP transport type, with the URL set to https://mcp.hubspot.com/, and enter your connector’s client ID and client secret.
149: Open the OAuth settings and complete the guided OAuth flow, which will direct you to authorize your HubSpot account.
150: Once authentication is complete, connect to the server and use the List Tools option to view available tools.
151: To verify your connection, run the get_user_details tool. A successful response will return information about your user, account, and available object and tool access.
152: General MCP client connection instructions
153: After creating your MCP connector, you can connect your MCP client to https://mcp.hubspot.com using your connector’s credentials. Your MCP client will need to handle the OAuth flow, including PKCE, to authenticate with HubSpot.
154: To configure your MCP client, you’ll need the following from your connector’s details page:
155: Client ID
156: Client secret
157: Redirect URL (must match what’s configured in your MCP client)
158: During the OAuth flow, you will:
159: Select the HubSpot account to connect.
160: Grant permissions to the connector. These permissions are based on the user’s permissions in HubSpot and determine what data the connector can access.
161: Authorize the connection.
162: Once authorized, your MCP client can make requests to the HubSpot MCP server on behalf of the authenticated user.
163: Not sure where to start with MCP clients? Check out this list of applications that support MCP integrations.
164: Troubleshooting
165: PKCE-related authentication failures
166: HubSpot’s MCP server requires PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) for all OAuth authentication flows. If your MCP client doesn’t handle PKCE automatically, you’ll need to implement it yourself:
167: Generate a random code_verifier (43-128 characters).
168: Derive the code_challenge from the verifier using the S256 method.
169: Include the code_challenge and code_challenge_method=S256 in the authorization request.
170: Include the code_verifier in the token exchange request.
171: If you see authentication errors during the OAuth flow, verify that your client is correctly generating and sending the PKCE parameters. Some MCP clients, like the MCP Inspector, handle PKCE automatically.
172: Token refresh failures
173: OAuth access tokens expire after a set period. If your MCP client stops working after a period of inactivity:
174: Ensure your client is using the refresh_token returned during the initial OAuth flow to request a new access token.
175: If the refresh token has also expired or been invalidated, you’ll need to re-run the full OAuth authorization flow.
176: Check that your redirect URL in the MCP client matches the redirect URL configured in your MCP connector in HubSpot.

34: OAuth implementation in apps
35: Apps use the Freshdesk REST APIs to access Freshdesk data (resources). API authentication is a process that verifies the identity of app users who want to access the Freshdesk data. API authentication ensures that only authorized users have access to the data.
36: We offer the following API authentication mechanisms to access Freshdesk resources:
37: Basic access authentication. For information on this, see API Authentication using API keys.
38: OAuth authorization and access token authentication. This section explains how your apps can use OAuth authorization.
39: Through OAuth authorization, the apps access the resources securely, without collecting or exposing sensitive credentials from the app user. Freshworks enables you to implement OAuth authorization flows in Freshworks apps and Custom apps.
40: Important:OAuth implementation is supported on all categories of apps: front-end, serverless, and SMI apps.
41: Notes:
42: Freshworks apps are built using the FDK and published to the Freshworks Marketplace. Custom apps are built using the FDK and are private to an organization.
43: In this document, any app (Freshworks or Custom) that uses OAuth flow is called an OAuth app.
44: The OAuth authorization and authentication flow, on successful implementation,
45: Enables app users to authorize the app to act on their behalf to access Freshdesk data.
46: Enables the app to request user's authorization and place a request for an access token.
47: Enables the app to obtain the access token and place authenticated REST API calls.

80: Freshdesk offers flexible pricing plans designed to scale with your business as it grows. Whether you’re starting with a single support channel or managing multichannel operations, our plans provide the flexibility to choose what fits your team’s size, budget, and complexity.
81: Prerequisites:
82: Ensure that you have account admin permissions to access the Plans & Billing page.
83: About our products and plans
84: We offer two core products that differ by capabilities and channel support:
85: Freshdesk Omni (Most Popular)
86: Freshdesk Omni is our multichannel support platform that allows you to manage customer interactions from email, chat, social media, and more, all from a unified inbox.
87: Freshdesk (Email-first)
88: Freshdesk is ideal for teams that primarily manage support through email. It provides the foundational ticketing, collaboration, and automation tools required to deliver efficient customer service.
89: Subscription plans
90: Both Freshdesk Omni and Freshdesk offer three flexible plans - Growth, Pro, and Enterprise. Each plan builds on the previous one, adding more customization, automation, and AI-powered features.
91: PlanIdeal forHighlights
92: Freshdesk Omni
93: Growth
94: Small and medium businesses
95: Includes knowledge base, automation, and basic reporting.
96: Pro
97: Scaling businesses
98: Adds advanced ticket routing, analytics dashboards, and WhatsApp campaigns.
99: Enterprise
100: Large organizations
101: Offers advanced customization, strong data security, audit logs, and AI capabilities.
102: Freshdesk
103: Growth
104: Small teams
105: Enables reporting, automation, and a self-service knowledge base.
106: Pro
107: Expanding teams
108: Adds advanced routing, custom roles, and stronger analytics.
109: Enterprise
110: Large teams
111: Adds advanced configuration, multiple SLAs, and enterprise-grade controls.
112: You can view the complete list of features in your Plans and Billing page or our Pricing Page.
113: Activate a plan
114: When you sign up for Freshdesk or Freshdesk Omni, you start with a 14-day trial that provides full access to all product features. After the trial, you can continue using the product by enrolling in the Free Program or by purchasing a paid plan.
115: Trial period
116: Every new account starts with a 14-day free trial that includes:
117: Full feature access: You can try automation, AI capabilities, analytics, and multichannel support.
118: Plan comparison: Switch between Growth, Pro, and Enterprise to determine which plan suits your business best.
119: Unlimited testing: Add agents, configure workflows, and explore integrations without restrictions.
120: During the trial period, you can track plan differences from either the Plans & Billing page within your account or the Pricing Page.
121: At the end of the trial, you can purchase any paid plan to continue seamlessly or move to the Free Program if you’re still evaluating.
122: Tip: If you wish to extend your trial period, please conatct your account manager or send an email to sales@freshdesk.com. For quick assistance, please include your account details (URL, company name) in the email.
123: Free program (Freshdesk only)
124: If you are a Freshdesk customer, you can switch to the Freshdesk Free Program and continue using the product at no cost for 6 months with a limited agent seat (two). The Free Program is specifically designed for small businesses and startups that want to manage customer communication while evaluating advanced features.
125: Note: The Free program applies only to Freshdesk customers and not available in Freshdesk Omni. Also, when you switch from a higher plan during the trial period to the Free Program, certain features and their configurations will be lost. For more information, see Explore Freshdesk Free Program.
126: To join the Free Program:
127: Log in to your Freshdesk account as an Account Admin and click Admin > Plans and Billing.
128: Click Switch plan.
129: Click Try out our Free Program.
130: Paid plans
131: Once you are ready to unlock advanced capabilities and scale your operations, you can choose a paid subscription. Each subscription plan is charged on a per-agent basis, and the total cost is determined by the number of agents in your account.
132: Note: Unless stated, the subscription charges do not include any taxes, levies, duties or similar governmental assessments, including value-added, sales, use or withholding taxes assessable by any local, state, provincial or foreign jurisdiction (collectively 'Taxes').
133: To purchase a paid plan:
134: Log in as an Account Admin and click Admin > Plans and Billing.
135: Click Switch plan.
136: Select the product (Freshdesk or Freshdesk Omni).
137: Select your preferred plan and click Proceed to payment.
138: Enter the number of agents.
139: Select the billing cycle. The options are monthly, annual, quarterly, or half-yearly subscriptions.
140: Select the currency.
141: Note: Only trial customers can change their currencies. After upgrading to a paid plan, your currency setting becomes fixed and cannot be modified via the Plan & Billing page. To request a change, contact billing@freshworks.com.
142: Click Add card and pay.
143: You can pay via credit cards, bank transfer, or PayPal (paypal@freshdesk.com). To use PayPal, ensure that you have a PayPal business ID.
144: Enter your billing information, card details, and click Subscribe.
145: Once payment is completed successfully, your plan becomes active right away. You can see your invoice on the Plans and Billing page, and a copy will be emailed to your registered email address. You may update your payment details anytime or contact us at billing@freshworks.com.
146: Manage subscriptions
147: Once you have purchased a plan and have an active subscription, you can view and manage all aspects of your product subscription directly from the Plans & Billing page.
148: You can:
149: Add more agents
150: Purchase add-ons
151: Upgrade or downgrade plans
152: Change billing cycles
153: View invoices
154: View subscription details
155: Log in as an Account Admin.
156: Go to Admin > Plans and Billing.
157: From this page, you can:
158: View your current plan details
159: Check billing frequency (monthly or annual)
160: Review active add-ons and agent count
161: Manage invoices and payment history
162: Auto-recharge subscription.
163: Add or remove agent seats
164: Your subscription cost is determined by the number of active agent seats in your plan.
165: Note: New agents can be added only if the payment mode is online. If you are paying offline, contact billing@freshworks.com.
166: When you add or remove agents:
167: Charges will be calculated pro rata for the remaining days in your billing cycle.
168: New agents are activated immediately once added.
169: When reducing the number of agents, ensure you delete the extra agents from your account first. The updated cost applies only after the extra agents are removed.
170: To add agent seats:
171: Go to Admin > Plans and Billing.
172: Click Manage Subscriptions.
173: Enter the number of additional agents you want to add.
174: Review the updated total price and click Update plan.
175: You can now invite and add more team members to your account. For details, see Add or Edit Support Agents.
176: To remove agent seats:
177: Before reducing seats, ensure you have removed extra agents from the agent configuration page so that you don’t exceed your available seats.
178: Go to Admin > Plans and Billing.
179: Click Manage Subscriptions and adjust the number of active agent seats.
180: Click Update plan.
181: View invoices
182: Your invoice will be automatically sent to your registered email address based on your billing cycle. Alternatively, you can view the invoice directly from the Plans & Billing page.
183: Note: This feature is available only for online payments that have a registered card on the portal. For accounts with offline modes of payment (bank transfers and PayPal), contact support@freshdesk.com.
184: To view your invoice:
185: Go to Admin > Plans and Billing.
186: In your current subscription plan card, click View Invoices.
187: You can view and download the invoices.
188: To change your email address, add the new email address in the right pane and click Update. You can add only one email address here.
189: Change billing cycle
190: You can choose to subscribe to paid plans on a monthly, quarterly, half-yearly, or annual basis. The billing date is automatically calculated from the subscription date. To change the date, contact billing@freshworks.com.
191: Go to Admin > Plans and Billing.
192: Click Manage Subscriptions.
193: Select the billing cycle from the top-right corner.
194: Click Update plan.
195: Purchase Freddy add-ons
196: Add-ons help you extend the functionality of your plan without changing your core plan tier. Freshdesk offers the following add-ons:
197: Freddy AI Agent
198: Freddy AI Copilot
199: For more details, see Manage Freddy AI Ad-ons.
200: Upgrade or downgrade plans
201: Easily switch to a higher or lower plan at any time, based on your business needs.
202: You can:
203: Upgrade to a higher plan: The upgrade will be applied immediately, and you’ll be charged a pro-rata amount for the remaining period in your current billing cycle.
204: Move to a lower plan: The change takes effect after your current billing cycle ends.
205: While switching plans, you can also update your agent count and add-ons (for example, Freddy AI Agent packs or Freddy Copilot agent licenses). When reducing the number of agents or removing add-ons, ensure you delete the extra agents from your account first.
206: For example, if you reduce your agent seats from 5 to 2, remove two agents from your account. The lower subscription cost applies only after the extra agents are removed.
207: Go to Admin > Plans and Billing.
208: Click Manage Subscriptions.
209: Switch to a higher or lower plan to upgrade or downgrade.

67: Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration in Freshdesk
68: Modified on: Mon, 5 Oct, 2026 at 11:37 AM
69: Applies to: Freshdesk, Freshdesk Omni 2026.
70: The Freshworks Model Context Protocol (MCP) server enables AI tools like Cursor and Claude to securely connect and interact with Freshdesk. The MCP server acts as middleware to expose specific capabilities, such as creating tickets, by using public APIs and supported authentication methods.
71: This article provides details about supported MCP integrations and how to configure them in your AI tools.
72: Note: Currently, Freshdesk allows you to authenticate requests involved in MCP integration by using an API key only.
73: TABLE OF CONTENTS
74: Supported plans and limits
75: Supported MCP integrations
76: Option 1: Set up MCP integration with Claude Code
77: Option 2: Set up MCP integration with Claude Desktop
78: Option 3: Set up MCP integration with Cursor
79: Option 4: Set up MCP integration with Microsoft Copilot Studio
80: Option 5: Set up MCP integration with Visual Studio Code
81: Troubleshoot issues
82: List of available tools
83: Pagination in MCP
84: Example prompts
85: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)
86: Freshworks MCP security
87: More resources
88: Supported plans and limits
89: This feature applies to the following products:
90: • Freshdesk Standalone 2021 (Latest version)
91: • Freshdesk Unified Omni 2026
92: Starting September 10, 2026, the Freshworks MCP integration is generally available. The rate limits and monthly action allowances for each plan are outlined below.
93: What counts as an MCP action?
94: An action is defined as a successful tool invocation via MCP. Examples of tool invocations. Examples:
95: • Fetch conversation related to the ticket with ID 1001 (1 action)
96: • Update the company name for the record with ID 11 to Apple (1 action)
97: Supported plans
98: Rate limits (actions per minute)
99: Included MCP actions (per account, annually)
100: Growth
101: 25
102: 1,200
103: Pro
104: 50
105: 6,000
106: Enterprise
107: 100
108: 12,000
109: Important:
110: • Pricing: To view current pricing and purchase add-on action packs, see Pricing.
111: • EAP transition:
112: • If you were on the Early Access Program (EAP), standard pricing and limits take effect on October 5, 2026.
113: • During the EAP, if you used the MCP integration on any plan other than Freshdesk Standalone 2021 (the latest version) or Freshdesk Unified Omni 2026 variant, the integration will stop working after September 10, 2026.
114: Supported MCP integrations
115: Freshdesk supports MCP integration with any AI tool that provides MCP support. This section highlights a selection of commonly used integrations that you can connect to Freshdesk.
116: Claude Code
117: Claude Desktop
118: Cursor
119: Microsoft Copilot Studio
120: Visual Studio Code
121: Option 1: Set up MCP integration with Claude Code
122: Connect and verify the MCP server within the Claude Code editor. After the setup is complete, Claude Code can use tools exposed by the MCP server directly within the editor.
123: Prerequisites
124: Before you begin, ensure you have the following:
125: The Claude Code app installed.
126: An active Claude account.
127: The Freshdesk MCP URL.
128: Note: Currently, custom domains are not supported for MCP endpoints. Ensure to use your Freshdesk base domain in the following format: https://<subdomain>.freshdesk.com/mcp
129: Create an MCP connection
130: To connect Claude Code to your MCP server, you must register the server using the http transport.
131: Run the following command in your terminal to register the Freshdesk MCP server:
132: claude mcp add my-remote-server --transport http https://<subdomain>.freshdesk.com/mcp --header "Authorization: <api-key>"
133: Expected output:
134: Added HTTP MCP server my-remote-server with URL: https://<subdomain>.freshdesk.com/mcp to local config
135: Headers: {
136: "Authorization": "<api-key>"
137: }
138: File modified: /Users/<username>/.claude.json [project: /Users/pmm]
139: Verify the connection
140: Use the following get command to confirm the server is listed as connected within the application:
141: claude mcp get my-remote-server
142: Expected output:
143: my-remote-server:
144: Scope: Local config (private to you in this project)
145: Status: ✓ Connected
146: Type: http
147: URL: https://<subdomain>.freshdesk.com/mcp
148: Headers:
149: Authorization: <api-key>
150: Option 2: Set up MCP integration with Claude Desktop
151: Connect and verify the MCP server within the Claude Desktop editor. After the setup is complete, Claude Desktop can use tools exposed by the MCP server directly within the editor.
152: Prerequisites
153: Before you begin, ensure you have the following:
154: The Claude Desktop app installed.
155: An active Claude account.
156: The Freshdesk MCP URL.
157: Note: Currently, custom domains are not supported for MCP endpoints. Ensure to use your Freshdesk base domain in the following format: https://<subdomain>.freshdesk.com/mcp
158: Create an MCP connection
159: To connect Claude Desktop to your MCP server, follow these steps:
160: Open Claude Desktop and go to Claude > Settings > Developer.
161: Select Edit Config. The claude_desktop_config.json file opens in your system's default text editor.
162: Copy and paste the following JSON configuration into the file. If other servers are already listed, add this as a new entry in the mcpServers object.
163: Note: Replace <mcp-url> with your specific server URL (for example, https://<subdomain>.freshdesk.com/mcp).
164: "mcpServers": {
165: "freshdesk-mcp": {
166: "command": "npx",
167: "args": [
168: "-y",
169: "mcp-remote",
170: "https://<subdomain>.freshdesk.com/mcp",
171: "--header",
172: "Authorization:<API_KEY>"
173: ]
174: }
175: }
176: Save the file and close the text editor.
177: Exit Claude Desktop by right-clicking the icon in the taskbar (Windows) or menu bar (macOS) and selecting Quit.
178: Relaunch Claude Desktop.
179: Follow the authentication prompts in your browser. After successful authentication, you can verify the connection status under Claude > Settings > Developer.
180: Option 3: Set up MCP integration with Cursor
181: Connect and verify the MCP server within the Cursor editor. After the setup is complete, Cursor can use tools exposed by the MCP server directly within the editor.
182: Prerequisites
183: Before you begin, ensure you have the following:
184: The Cursor app installed.
185: An active Cursor account.
186: The Freshdesk MCP URL.
187: Note: Currently, custom domains are not supported for MCP endpoints. Ensure to use your Freshdesk base domain in the following format: https://<subdomain>.freshdesk.com/mcp
188: Create an MCP connection
189: To connect Cursor to the MCP server, add the server details to your application's configuration file. To do so, follow these steps:
190: Open Cursor and go to the root folder of your project or user home directory for global configuration.
191: Create or update the .cursor/mcp.json file.
192: Add the following JSON object to the file:
193: Sample configuration using API key
194: {
195: "mcpServers": {
196: "freshdesk": {
197: "type": "http",
198: "url": "https://<subdomain>.freshdesk.com/mcp",
199: "headers": {
200: "Authorization": "<API-KEY>"
201: }
202: }
203: }
204: }
205: The following table describes the attributes used to configure the MCP server:
206: Attribute name
207: Description
208: mcpServers
209: List of all MCP servers to which the Cursor should connect.
210: Attribute of the mcpServers object
211: <name_of_the_MCP_object>
212: The unique name for your MCP server object.
213: Attribute of the <name_of_the_MCP_object> object
214: type
215: The protocol used by the MCP client to communicate with the MCP server.
216: url
217: The endpoint used by the MCP client to connect to your MCP server.
218: headers
219: Custom HTTP headers that the MCP client must send when connecting to your MCP server.
220: Note: Freshdesk supports authorization via API key only. In your configuration, include the "Authorization": "<YOUR_API_KEY>" attribute and replace <YOUR_API_KEY> with your actual Freshdesk API key.
221: Verify the configuration
222: After you save the configuration file, follow these steps to verify that Cursor can access the server and its tools:
223: In Cursor, go to View > Command Palette
224: Enter View: Open MCP Settings and select it from the list.
225: On the Tools page, locate the Installed MCP Servers section and verify your server name appears.
226: To view the available tools, expand the server card.
227: Once the connection is established, Cursor automatically retrieves the tools. You can invoke them through natural language prompts or allow Cursor to suggest them based on your current task.
228: If the server is offline or the configuration is incorrect, Cursor displays an error message provided by the MCP server in the settings view.
229: Option 4: Set up MCP integration with Microsoft Copilot Studio
230: Connect and verify the MCP server within the Microsoft Copilot Studio editor. After the setup is complete, Microsoft Copilot Studio can use tools exposed by the MCP server directly within the editor.
231: Prerequisites
232: Before you begin, ensure you have the following:
233: The Microsoft Copilot Studio app installed.
234: An active Microsoft Copilot Studio account.
235: An existing agent created within Microsoft Copilot Studio.
236: The Freshdesk MCP URL.
237: Note: Currently, custom domains are not supported for MCP endpoints. Ensure to use your Freshdesk base domain in the following format: https://<subdomain>.freshdesk.com/mcp
238: Create an MCP connection
239: To link Copilot Studio to your MCP server, follow these steps:
240: In the Copilot Studio dashboard, select Agents from the left navigation pane.
241: Select your agent from the list.
242: Open the Tools page for the agent.
243: Click + Add a tool at the top left of the page.
244: The Add tool window appears.
245: Select + New tool > Model Context Protocol.
246: The Add a Model Context Protocol server window appears.
247: Enter the following details:
248: Server name: Enter a name for the server.
249: Server description: Provide a short description of why the server is required.
250: Server URL: Enter the endpoint where the MCP client can reach your MCP server. For example, https://<subdomain>.freshdesk.com/mcp.
251: Authentication: Select the authentication mode as API key
252: Click Create.
253: After successful creation, the Add tool window appears to configure the connection.
254: In the Connection dropdown, you will see No connections available.
255: Click the dropdown and select Create new connection > Create.
256: In the authorization window, select your account name and click Continue.
257: After authorization succeeds, click Add and configure on the Add tool window.
258: You are redirected to the page for the newly created tool. Under the Tools section, you can view the list of available tools.
259: Verify the MCP connection
260: To confirm that your agent is actively connected to the Freshworks MCP server, follow these steps:
261: Go to your agent in Copilot Studio by selecting Agents and choosing the agent you want to verify.
262: The agent overview page opens.
263: Select Settings to open the agent settings page.
264: In the left navigation pane, select Connection Settings.
265: A table displays all connections associated with your agent.
266: For the newly configured connection, if the status is Not connected, click Connect.
267: The Create or pick a connection window appears.
268: Select the newly created connection and click Submit.
269: The status updates to Connected once the link is successfully established.
270: Option 5: Set up MCP integration with Visual Studio Code
271: Connect and verify the MCP server within the Visual Studio Code editor . After the setup is complete, Visual Studio Code can use tools exposed by the MCP server directly within the editor.
272: Prerequisites
273: Before you begin, ensure you have the following:
274: The Visual Studio Code app installed.
275: The MCP extension for VS Code installed.
276: The Freshdesk MCP URL.
277: Note: Currently, custom domains are not supported for MCP endpoints. Ensure to use your Freshdesk base domain in the following format: https://<subdomain>.freshdesk.com/mcp
278: Create an MCP connection
279: To integrate the MCP server into your VS Code environment, follow these steps:
280: Launch VS Code.
281: Open the Command Palette by pressing Ctrl+Shift+P (Windows) or Cmd+Shift+P (macOS).
282: Enter and select MCP: Open User Configuration.
283: Add the following JSON object to the mcp.json file and save it.
284: {
285: "servers": {
286: "my-remote-server": {
287: "type": "http",
288: "url": "https://<subdomain>.freshdesk.com/mcp",
289: "headers": {
290: "Authorization": "<api-key>"
291: }
292: }
293: }
294: }
295: A Start button appears above the my-remote-server entry. Click Start to initialize the server.
296: The following output appears to confirm the server is active:
297: Verify the configuration
298: After setting up your connection, you can confirm the server is running using either of the following methods:
299: View active servers: Open the Command Palette and select MCP: List Servers. Ensure your Freshdesk server is listed as active.
300: Review raw config: Open your mcp.json file to verify the server details and configuration target.
301: You can now run MCP-specific commands directly within your VS Code terminal or command palette to interact with Freshdesk data.
302: Troubleshoot issues
303: Issue: Connection failures
304: If the connection verification fails, check the following:
305: Network: Check your active internet connection and VPN status.
306: URL Accessibility: Open https://<subdomain>.freshdesk.com/mcp in your browser to ensure the endpoint is live.
307: Authentication: Verify that a valid API key is included in the authorization header.
308: Issue: MCP connection fails due to IP restrictions
309: Symptoms
310: MCP server connection fails despite correct endpoint configuration
311: Timeout or connection refused errors when running mcp-remote
312: Connection works in some networks but fails in restricted environments
313: Possible cause
314: Your Freshdesk or your organization’s network, enforces IP restrictions that block requests to or from the MCP server. If the required IP ranges are not allowlisted, the connection cannot be established.
315: Resolution
316: Allowlist required IP ranges:
317: Add the following IP ranges to your allowlist based on your data center/region:
318: Core ranges
319: AU: 10.3.0.0/16
320: IN: 10.44.0.0/16
321: EUC: 10.113.0.0/16
322: USE: 10.111.0.0/16, 10.113.0.0/16
323: EUN: 10.96.80.0/20
324: Additional ranges
325: US:
326: 10.17.144.0/20
327: 10.25.128.0/18
328: EUC:
329: 10.17.104.0/21
330: 10.25.192.0/18
331: IN:
332: 10.17.128.0/20
333: AU:
334: 10.17.96.0/21
335: EUN:
336: 10.97.216.0/21
337: Update IP restriction settings:
338: Configure IP restrictions in your Freshworks account.
339: Verify network access:
340: Ensure outbound HTTPS (port 443) is allowed
341: Confirm no firewall or proxy is blocking these IP ranges
342: Retry the connection:
343: Run: npx -y mcp-remote https://<subdomain>.freshdesk.com/mcp
344: Verification
345: MCP connection succeeds without timeout or network errors
346: MCP client shows the server status as Connected
347: Next steps
348: If the issue persists after allowlisting:
349: Verify region alignment between your Freshdesk account and configured IP ranges
350: Check with your network administrator for additional firewall or proxy restrictions

467: Pagination in MCP
468: When an MCP tool returns many results, such as a list of solution articles, sending the entire payload at once can exceed token limits or cause the LLM to truncate the data. Large payloads can also slow down response times and reduce the accuracy of the AI.
469: To prevent this, the MCP server uses pagination to deliver results in smaller, manageable batches. This ensures the LLM processes information efficiently while staying within its operational limits.
470: The pagination process provides the following benefits:
471: Automatic processing: The MCP client and the LLM handle subsequent data requests automatically using the nextCursor parameter.
472: No manual configuration: You don't need to manage page numbers, cursors, or page sizes manually.
473: Optimized performance: Smaller response batches ensure more reliable processing and faster response times from the AI tool.
474: Example prompts
475: You can use the following prompts to interact with the Freshdesk MCP server through your AI tool. These are samples only; you can modify them to suit your specific requirements.
476: Manage tickets:
477: "Create a high-priority ticket for a payment issue from Sarah."
478: "Get all tickets created today and group them by status."
479: "Filter my assigned tickets for those with 'open' status and 'high' priority."
480: Manage users and groups:
481: "Create a contact for John Doe with the email johndoe@acme-corp.com."
482: "Add a new support group called 'Network Team'."
483: "Show me the members of the Network Team group."
484: Manage companies and articles:
485: "Create a company named 'Acme Corp'."
486: "Find the solution article for payment refunds."

416: outlined_flag
417: Google Ads API utilizes the OAuth 2.0 protocol for authentication and authorization, allowing your app to access user accounts without handling login information.
418: In addition to OAuth 2.0 credentials, a developer token is also required to make Google Ads API calls.
419: While all Google-supported OAuth 2.0 scenarios work, this guide focuses on the most common ones for Google Ads API developers.
420: The recommended OAuth 2.0 approach depends on your specific application scenario, such as integrating with existing Google APIs, managing your own accounts, or managing accounts on behalf of other users.
421: Note: You should configure your OAuth credentials using the same Google Cloud
422: project where you have enabled the
423: Google Ads API and requested an appropriate
424: API access level for the Google Ads API to work
425: correctly.
426: Just like other Google APIs, Google Ads API uses the OAuth 2.0 protocol
427: for authentication and authorization. OAuth 2.0 enables your Google Ads API client app
428: to access a user's Google Ads account without having to handle or store the user's
429: login info.
430: Broadly speaking, all the OAuth 2.0 authorization scenarios
431: that Google supports also work with Google Ads API. However, this guide focuses on the
432: scenarios that are most common for Google Ads API developers.
433: Scenario
434: Recommended approach
435: My app already uses one or more Google APIs. I have already built support
436: for OAuth 2.0 workflows for my app, and just need to add Google Ads API
437: functionality to my existing app.
438: Make sure your authorized user or your service account has access to
439: the Google Ads accounts you are making API calls to. For more
440: information, see the
441: Google Ads access model.
442: See the
443: multi-user
444: authentication workflow or the
445: service account workflow
446: depending on the approach you are using with the rest of the Google
447: APIs that your app is using.
448: I am building an app that manages Google Ads accounts that I already have
449: access to. If I need to manage new Google Ads accounts in the future, I will
450: gain access to those accounts by linking them under my Google Ads manager
451: account.
452: OR
453: Someone will
454: invite
455: me to manage those accounts.
456: Use the service account
457: workflow.
458: If your organizational policies or account setup prevent you from using
459: service accounts, use the
460: single-user
461: authentication workflow instead.
462: I am building an app that manages Google Ads accounts on behalf of other
463: users. My app will build a user screen that lets the signed-in users
464: connect to their Google Ads accounts and authorize my app to manage those
465: accounts on their behalf.
466: Use multi-user
467: authentication.

469: Google Account, visit your Google Account permissions page.
