24: Usage
25: Search for only one user:
26: sherlock user123
27: Search for multiples users:
28: sherlock user1 user2 user3
29: Accounts found will be stored in an individual text file with the corresponding username (e.g user123.txt).
30: $ sherlock --help
31: usage: sherlock [-h] [--version] [--verbose] [--folderoutput FOLDEROUTPUT]
32: [--output OUTPUT] [--tor] [--unique-tor] [--csv] [--xlsx]
33: [--site SITE_NAME] [--proxy PROXY_URL] [--json JSON_FILE]
34: [--timeout TIMEOUT] [--print-all] [--print-found] [--no-color]
35: [--browse] [--local] [--nsfw]
36: USERNAMES [USERNAMES ...]
37: Sherlock: Find Usernames Across Social Networks (Version 0.14.3)
38: positional arguments:
39: USERNAMES One or more usernames to check with social networks.
40: Check similar usernames using {?} (replace to '_', '-', '.').
41: optional arguments:
42: -h, --help show this help message and exit
43: --version Display version information and dependencies.
44: --verbose, -v, -d, --debug
45: Display extra debugging information and metrics.
46: --folderoutput FOLDEROUTPUT, -fo FOLDEROUTPUT
47: If using multiple usernames, the output of the results will be
48: saved to this folder.
49: --output OUTPUT, -o OUTPUT
50: If using single username, the output of the result will be saved
51: to this file.
52: --tor, -t Make requests over Tor; increases runtime; requires Tor to be
53: installed and in system path.
54: --unique-tor, -u Make requests over Tor with new Tor circuit after each request;
55: increases runtime; requires Tor to be installed and in system
56: path.
57: --csv Create Comma-Separated Values (CSV) File.
58: --xlsx Create the standard file for the modern Microsoft Excel
59: spreadsheet (xlsx).
60: --site SITE_NAME Limit analysis to just the listed sites. Add multiple options to
61: specify more than one site.
62: --proxy PROXY_URL, -p PROXY_URL
63: Make requests over a proxy. e.g. socks5://127.0.0.1:1080
64: --json JSON_FILE, -j JSON_FILE
65: Load data from a JSON file or an online, valid, JSON file.
66: --timeout TIMEOUT Time (in seconds) to wait for response to requests (Default: 60)
67: --print-all Output sites where the username was not found.
68: --print-found Output sites where the username was found.
69: --no-color Don't color terminal output
70: --browse, -b Browse to all results on default browser.
71: --local, -l Force the use of the local data.json file.
72: --nsfw Include checking of NSFW sites from default list.

140: Preview
141: This feature is
142: subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the
143: Service Specific
144: Terms.
145: Pre-GA features are available "as is" and might have limited support.
146: For more information, see the
147: launch stage descriptions.
148: Gemini Notebook Enterprise is a powerful tool for generating insights and
149: summaries from your documents. This page describes the APIs that let you
150: perform the following notebook management tasks programmatically:
151: Create a notebook
152: Retrieve a notebook
153: List recently viewed notebooks
154: Delete a notebook
155: Share a notebook
156: Before you begin
157: Before you start working with your notebooks, do the following:
158: Set up Gemini Notebook Enterprise.
159: Get licenses for Gemini Notebook Enterprise
160: and assign a license to your user account.
161: Grant the Cloud NotebookLM User role
162: (roles/discoveryengine.notebookLmUser) to your user account.
163: In a local terminal or Cloud Shell, sign in to the
164: Google Cloud CLI with your user credentials by running
165: the gcloud auth login command:
166: gcloud auth login
167: Signing in with your user credentials ensures that
168: gcloud auth print-access-token generates an access token for your user
169: account. The projects.locations.notebooks REST
170: API methods on
171: this page require an authenticated user account with an active
172: Gemini Notebook Enterprise license.
173: Use the US multi-regional endpoint
174: If your Gemini Notebook Enterprise subscription is in the US
175: multi-region, you can send the requests on this page to the US multi-regional
176: endpoint, discoveryengine.us.rep.googleapis.com. A multi-regional endpoint
177: processes your requests and terminates TLS within the multi-region, so your
178: request data stays in the US while it's in transit. Using this endpoint doesn't
179: change where your notebooks are stored. For more information, see
180: Regional and multi-regional API endpoints
181: overview in the Google Cloud
182: security guide.
183: To use the US multi-regional endpoint, make the following changes to each
184: request URL on this page:
185: Replace the
186: ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com
187: host with discoveryengine.us.rep.googleapis.com.
188: Set LOCATION to us.
189: The rest of each request stays the same. To learn how you choose your
190: subscription's multi-region, see
191: Get a subscription.
192: For the list of regional and multi-regional service endpoints, see
193: Regional and multi-regional service endpoints
194: in the Virtual Private Cloud guide.
195: Create a notebook
196: To create a new notebook, use the
197: notebooks.create
198: method.
199: REST
200: curl -X POST \
201: -H "Authorization:Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
202: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
203: "https://ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks" \
204: -d '{
205: "title": "NOTEBOOK_TITLE",
206: }'
207: Replace the following:
208: ENDPOINT_LOCATION: the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following
209: values:
210: us for the US multi-region
211: eu for the EU multi-region
212: global for the Global location
213: For more information, see
214: Specify a multi-region
215: for your data store.
216: PROJECT_NUMBER: the number of your Google Cloud project.
217: LOCATION:
218: the geographic location of your data store, such as global.
219: For more information, see Locations.
220: NOTEBOOK_TITLE: a UTF-8 encoded string used as a
221: title for the notebook that you want to create.
222: If the request is successful, you should receive a JSON similar to the
223: following.
224: {
225: "title": "NOTEBOOK_TITLE",
226: "notebookId": "NOTEBOOK_ID",
227: "emoji": "",
228: "metadata": {
229: "userRole": "PROJECT_ROLE_OWNER",
230: "isShared": false,
231: "isShareable": true
232: },
233: "name": "NOTEBOOK_NAME"
234: }
235: Note the following:
236: NOTEBOOK_ID: a unique ID to identify
237: the created notebook. You need the notebook ID for other notebook management
238: tasks, such as sharing or retrieving.
239: NOTEBOOK_NAME: the complete resource name of the
240: notebook. This field has the following pattern:
241: projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks/NOTEBOOK_ID
242: Access the created notebook and get its ID in a browser
243: To access the created notebook and get its ID using a browser, do the following.
244: Go to the Gemini Notebook Enterprise homepage that's available at one of
245: the following URLs:
246: If you're using a Google identity, go to:
247: https://notebook.cloud.google.com/LOCATION/?project=PROJECT_NUMBER
248: If you're using a third-party identity, go to:
249: https://notebook.cloud.google/LOCATION/?project=PROJECT_NUMBER
250: Select the created notebook. The URL of the selected notebook has the following pattern:
251: If you're using a Google identity:
252: https://notebook.cloud.google.com/LOCATION/notebook/NOTEBOOK_ID?project=PROJECT_NUMBER
253: If you're using a third-party identity:
254: https://notebook.cloud.google/LOCATION/notebook/NOTEBOOK_ID?project=PROJECT_NUMBER
255: Note the URL and the notebook ID, which are useful for other notebook
256: management tasks, such as sharing.
257: Retrieve a notebook
258: To retrieve a specific notebook using its notebook ID, use the
259: notebooks.get
260: method.
261: REST
262: curl -X GET \
263: -H "Authorization:Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
264: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
265: "https://ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks/NOTEBOOK_ID"
266: Replace the following:
267: ENDPOINT_LOCATION: the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following
268: values:
269: us for the US multi-region
270: eu for the EU multi-region
271: global for the Global location
272: For more information, see
273: Specify a multi-region
274: for your data store.
275: PROJECT_NUMBER: the number of your Google Cloud project.
276: LOCATION:
277: the geographic location of your data store, such as global.
278: For more information, see Locations.
279: NOTEBOOK_ID: the notebook's unique identifier
280: that you received when you created the notebook.
281: If the request is successful, you should get a JSON response similar to the
282: following for an empty notebook. If you call this method after you
283: add sources to your notebook, you
284: receive details about all the sources added to the retrieved notebook. If you
285: have configured CMEK
286: details,
287: you also receive CMEK-related information for the notebook.
288: {
289: "title": "NOTEBOOK_TITLE",
290: "notebookId": "NOTEBOOK_ID",
291: "emoji": "",
292: "metadata": {
293: "userRole": "PROJECT_ROLE_OWNER",
294: "isShared": false,
295: "isShareable": true,
296: "lastViewed": "LAST_VIEWED_TIME",
297: "createTime": "LAST_CREATED_TIME"
298: },
299: "name": "NOTEBOOK_NAME"
300: }
301: List recently viewed notebooks
302: To get a list of all notebooks in a project that were recently viewed, use the
303: notebooks.listRecentlyViewed
304: method. By default, the response lists the last 500 notebooks. You can choose
305: to paginate the responses with the pageSize query parameter.
306: REST
307: curl -X GET \
308: -H "Authorization:Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
309: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
310: "https://ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks:listRecentlyViewed"
311: Replace the following:
312: ENDPOINT_LOCATION: the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following
313: values:
314: us for the US multi-region
315: eu for the EU multi-region
316: global for the Global location
317: For more information, see
318: Specify a multi-region
319: for your data store.
320: PROJECT_NUMBER: the number of your Google Cloud project.
321: LOCATION:
322: the geographic location of your data store, such as global.
323: For more information, see Locations.
324: If the request is successful, you should get a JSON response similar to the
325: following. The response contains up to last 500 notebooks that a user
326: accessed recently.
327: {
328: "notebooks": [
329: {
330: "title": "NOTEBOOK_TITLE_1",
331: "notebookId": "NOTEBOOK_ID_1",
332: "emoji": "",
333: "metadata": {
334: "userRole": "PROJECT_ROLE_OWNER",
335: "isShared": false,
336: "isShareable": true,
337: "lastViewed": "LAST_VIEWED_TIME",
338: "createTime": "LAST_CREATED_TIME"
339: },
340: "name": "NOTEBOOK_NAME_1"
341: },
342: {
343: "title": "NOTEBOOK_TITLE_2",
344: "notebookId": "NOTEBOOK_ID_2",
345: "emoji": "",
346: "metadata": {
347: "userRole": "PROJECT_ROLE_OWNER",
348: "isShared": false,
349: "isShareable": true,
350: "lastViewed": "LAST_VIEWED_TIME",
351: "createTime": "LAST_CREATED_TIME"
352: },
353: "name": "NOTEBOOK_NAME_2"
354: }
355: ]
356: }
357: Delete a notebook
358: To delete a notebook, use the
359: notebooks.batchDelete
360: method.
361: REST
362: curl -X POST \
363: -H "Authorization:Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
364: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
365: "https://ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks:batchDelete" \
366: -d '{
367: "names": [
368: "NOTEBOOK_NAME"
369: ]
370: }'
371: Replace the following:
372: ENDPOINT_LOCATION: the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following
373: values:
374: us for the US multi-region
375: eu for the EU multi-region
376: global for the Global location
377: For more information, see
378: Specify a multi-region
379: for your data store.
380: PROJECT_NUMBER: the number of your Google Cloud project.
381: LOCATION:
382: the geographic location of your data store, such as global.
383: For more information, see Locations.
384: NOTEBOOK_NAME: the complete resource name of the
385: notebook to be deleted. This field has the pattern:
386: projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks/NOTEBOOK_ID.
387: If the request is successful, you receive an empty JSON object. If the
388: notebook doesn't exist, you also receive an empty JSON object, so make
389: sure to specify the notebook name correctly.
390: Share a notebook
391: To share a new notebook, use the
392: notebooks.share
393: method.
394: The user with whom you want to share the notebook must be granted the
395: Cloud NotebookLM User role.
396: REST
397: In your Google Cloud project, assign the Cloud NotebookLM User
398: Identity and Access Management (IAM) role to the users with whom you want to share the
399: notebook.
400: Call the following method.
401: curl -X POST \
402: -H "Authorization:Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
403: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
404: "https://ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks/NOTEBOOK_ID:share" \
405: -d '{
406: "accountAndRoles": [
407: {
408: "email":"USER_EMAIL_1",
409: "role":"USER_ROLE_1",
410: },
411: {
412: "email":"USER_EMAIL_2",
413: "role":"USER_ROLE_2",
414: },
415: ]
416: }'
417: Replace the following:
418: ENDPOINT_LOCATION: the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following
419: values:
420: us for the US multi-region
421: eu for the EU multi-region
422: global for the Global location
423: For more information, see
424: Specify a multi-region
425: for your data store.
426: PROJECT_NUMBER: the number of your Google Cloud project.
427: LOCATION:
428: the geographic location of your data store, such as global.
429: For more information, see Locations.
430: NOTEBOOK_ID: a unique ID to identify
431: the notebook that you want to share. You need the notebook ID for other notebook management
432: tasks, such as sharing or retrieving.
433: USER_EMAIL: the email address of the user with whom
434: you want to share the notebook.
435: USER_ROLE: a role that you want to assign to
436: the user. It can be one of the following:
437: PROJECT_ROLE_WRITER: The user has write permissions on the project.
438: PROJECT_ROLE_READER: The user has read permissions on the project.
439: PROJECT_ROLE_NOT_SHARED:The user has no access to the project.
440: If the request is successful, you receive an empty JSON object.
441: Note: You can't assign PROJECT_ROLE_OWNER with this method. The
442: account that creates a notebook is its owner, and ownership can't be
443: transferred.
444: Verify users using a browser
445: To verify whether you've shared the notebook with the correct users and
446: assigned them correct roles, do the following:
447: Open the notebook in your browser. A notebook has the following URL pattern:
448: If you're using a Google identity:
449: https://notebook.cloud.google.com/LOCATION/notebook/NOTEBOOK_ID?project=PROJECT_NUMBER
450: If you're using a third-party identity:

137: Add and manage data sources in a notebook (API)
138: Stay organized with collections
139: Save and categorize content based on your preferences.
140: Preview
141: This feature is
142: subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the
143: Service Specific
144: Terms.
145: Pre-GA features are available "as is" and might have limited support.
146: For more information, see the
147: launch stage descriptions.
148: After you have created your notebook, you can add various content types to it as
149: data sources. You can do so in batches or as single files. Some of the sources
150: include Google Docs, Google Slides, raw text, web content, and YouTube
151: videos.
152: This page describes how to perform the following tasks:
153: Add data sources in a batch
154: Upload a file as a source
155: Retrieve a source
156: Delete data sources from a notebook
157: Before you begin
158: If you plan to add Google Docs or Google Slides as your data source,
159: you must authorize access to Google Drive using Google user credentials. To
160: do so, run the following
161: gcloud auth login
162: command and follow the instructions in the CLI.
163: gcloud auth login --enable-gdrive-access
164: Use the US multi-regional endpoint
165: If your Gemini Notebook Enterprise subscription is in the US
166: multi-region, you can send the requests on this page to the US multi-regional
167: endpoint, discoveryengine.us.rep.googleapis.com. A multi-regional endpoint
168: processes your requests and terminates TLS within the multi-region, so your
169: request data stays in the US while it's in transit. Using this endpoint doesn't
170: change where your notebooks are stored. For more information, see
171: Regional and multi-regional API endpoints
172: overview in the Google Cloud
173: security guide.
174: To use the US multi-regional endpoint, make the following changes to each
175: request URL on this page:
176: Replace the
177: ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com
178: host with discoveryengine.us.rep.googleapis.com.
179: Set LOCATION to us.
180: The rest of each request stays the same. To learn how you choose your
181: subscription's multi-region, see
182: Get a subscription.
183: For the list of regional and multi-regional service endpoints, see
184: Regional and multi-regional service endpoints
185: in the Virtual Private Cloud guide.
186: Add data sources in a batch
187: To add sources to a notebook, call the
188: notebooks.sources.batchCreate
189: method.
190: REST
191: curl -X POST \
192: -H "Authorization:Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
193: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
194: "https://ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks/NOTEBOOK_ID/sources:batchCreate" \
195: -d '{
196: "userContents": [
197: {
198: USER_CONTENT
199: }
200: ]
201: }'
202: Replace the following:
203: ENDPOINT_LOCATION: the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following
204: values:
205: us for the US multi-region
206: eu for the EU multi-region
207: global for the Global location
208: For more information, see
209: Specify a multi-region
210: for your data store.
211: PROJECT_NUMBER: the number of your Google Cloud project.
212: LOCATION:
213: the geographic location of your data store, such as global.
214: For more information, see Locations.
215: NOTEBOOK_ID: The unique identifier of the notebook.
216: USER_CONTENT: The data source content.
217: You can add only one of the following data sources as your content:
218: For Google Drive content consisting of Google Docs or Google Slides,
219: add:
220: "googleDriveContent": {
221: "documentId": "DOCUMENT_ID_GOOGLE",
222: "mimeType": "MIME_TYPE",
223: "sourceName": "DISPLAY_NAME_GOOGLE"
224: }
225: Replace the following:
226: DOCUMENT_ID_GOOGLE: the ID of the file that's
227: in the Google Drive. This ID appears in the URL of the file. To get the
228: document ID of a file, open the file. Its URL has the pattern:
229: https://docs.google.com/FILE_TYPE/d/DOCUMENT_ID_GOOGLE/edit?resourcekey=RESOURCE_KEY.
230: MIME_TYPE: the mime type of the selected
231: document. Use application/vnd.google-apps.document for
232: Google Docs or application/vnd.google-apps.presentation
233: for Google Slides.
234: DISPLAY_NAME_GOOGLE: the display name of the
235: data source.
236: For raw text input, add:
237: "textContent": {
238: "sourceName": "DISPLAY_NAME_TEXT",
239: "content": "TEXT_CONTENT"
240: }
241: Replace the following:
242: DISPLAY_NAME_TEXT: the display name of the
243: data source.
244: TEXT_CONTENT: the raw text content that you want
245: to upload as a data source.
246: For web content, add:
247: "webContent": {
248: "url": "URL_WEBCONTENT",
249: "sourceName": "DISPLAY_NAME_WEB"
250: }
251: Replace the following:
252: URL_WEBCONTENT: the URL of the content that you
253: want to upload as a data source.
254: DISPLAY_NAME_WEB: the display name of the
255: data source.
256: For video content, add:
257: "videoContent": {
258: "youtubeUrl": "URL_YOUTUBE"
259: }
260: Replace URL_YOUTUBE with the URL of the YouTube
261: video that you want to upload as a data source.
262: If the request is successful, you should get an instance of the
263: source
264: object as a response, similar to the following JSON. Note the
265: SOURCE_ID and
266: SOURCE_RESOURCE_NAME, which are required to perform
267: other tasks, such as retrieving or deleting the data source.
268: {
269: "sources": [
270: {
271: "sourceId": {
272: "id": "SOURCE_ID"
273: },
274: "title": "DISPLAY_NAME",
275: "metadata": {
276: "xyz": "abc"
277: },
278: "settings": {
279: "status": "SOURCE_STATUS_COMPLETE"
280: },
281: "name": "SOURCE_RESOURCE_NAME"
282: }
283: ]
284: }
285: Upload a file as a source
286: In addition to adding data sources in batches, you can upload single files
287: that can be used as data sources in your notebook.
288: To upload a single file, call the
289: notebooks.sources.uploadFile method.
290: REST
291: curl -X POST --data-binary "@PATH/TO/FILE" \
292: -H "Authorization:Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
293: -H "X-Goog-Upload-File-Name: FILE_DISPLAY_NAME" \
294: -H "X-Goog-Upload-Protocol: raw" \
295: -H "Content-Type: CONTENT_TYPE" \
296: "https://ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com/upload/v1alpha/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks/NOTEBOOK_ID/sources:uploadFile" \
297: Replace the following:
298: PATH/TO/FILE: the path to the file that you want
299: to upload.
300: FILE_DISPLAY_NAME: a string that denotes the
301: display name of the file in the notebook.
302: CONTENT_TYPE: the type of content that you want to
303: upload. For a list of supported content types, see
304: Supported content types.
305: ENDPOINT_LOCATION: the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following
306: values:
307: us for the US multi-region
308: eu for the EU multi-region
309: global for the Global location
310: For more information, see
311: Specify a multi-region
312: for your data store.
313: PROJECT_NUMBER: the number of your Google Cloud project.
314: LOCATION:
315: the geographic location of your data store, such as global.
316: For more information, see Locations.
317: NOTEBOOK_ID: the unique identifier of the notebook.
318: If the request is successful, you should get a JSON response similar to the
319: following.
320: {
321: "sourceId": {
322: "id": "SOURCE_ID"
323: }
324: }
325: Supported content types
326: The file that you upload as a source must be supported.
327: The following document content types are supported:
328: File extension
329: Content type
330: .pdf
331: application/pdf
332: .txt
333: text/plain
334: .md
335: text/markdown
336: .docx
337: application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document
338: .pptx
339: application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.presentationml.presentation
340: .xlsx
341: application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet
342: The following audio content types are supported:
343: File extension
344: Content type
345: .3g2
346: audio/3gpp2
347: .3gp
348: audio/3gpp
349: .aac
350: audio/aac
351: .aif
352: audio/aiff
353: .aifc
354: audio/aiff
355: .aiff
356: audio/aiff
357: .amr
358: audio/amr
359: .au
360: audio/basic
361: .avi
362: video/x-msvideo
363: .cda
364: application/x-cdf
365: .m4a
366: audio/m4a
367: .mid
368: audio/midi
369: .midi
370: audio/midi
371: .mp3
372: audio/mpeg
373: .mp4
374: video/mp4
375: .mpeg
376: audio/mpeg
377: .ogg
378: audio/ogg
379: .opus
380: audio/ogg
381: .ra
382: audio/vnd.rn-realaudio
383: .ram
384: audio/vnd.rn-realaudio
385: .snd
386: audio/basic
387: .wav
388: audio/wav
389: .weba
390: audio/webm
391: .wma
392: audio/x-ms-wma
393: The following image content types are supported:
394: File extension
395: Content type
396: .png
397: image/png
398: .jpg
399: image/jpg
400: .jpeg
401: image/jpeg
402: Retrieve a source
403: To retrieve a specific source that's added to a notebook, use the
404: notebooks.sources.get
405: method.
406: REST
407: curl -X GET \
408: -H "Authorization:Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
409: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
410: "https://ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks/NOTEBOOK_ID/sources/SOURCE_ID"
411: Replace the following:
412: ENDPOINT_LOCATION: the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following
413: values:
414: us for the US multi-region
415: eu for the EU multi-region
416: global for the Global location
417: For more information, see
418: Specify a multi-region
419: for your data store.
420: PROJECT_NUMBER: the number of your Google Cloud project.
421: LOCATION:
422: the geographic location of your data store, such as global.
423: For more information, see Locations.
424: NOTEBOOK_ID: the unique identifier
425: that you received when you created the notebook. For more information, see
426: Create a notebook.
427: SOURCE_ID: the source's identifier
428: that you received when you added the source to your notebook.
429: If the request is successful, you should get a JSON response similar to the following.
430: {
431: "sources": [
432: {
433: "sourceId": {
434: "id": "SOURCE_ID"
435: },
436: "title": "DISPLAY_NAME",
437: "metadata": {
438: "wordCount": 148,
439: "tokenCount": 160
440: },
441: "settings": {
442: "status": "SOURCE_STATUS_COMPLETE"
443: },
444: "name": "SOURCE_RESOURCE_NAME"
445: }
446: ]
447: }
448: Delete data sources from a notebook
449: To delete data sources in bulk from a notebook, use the
450: notebooks.sources.batchDelete
451: method.
452: REST
453: curl -X POST \
454: -H "Authorization:Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
455: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
456: "https://ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks/NOTEBOOK_ID/sources:batchDelete" \
457: -d '{
458: "names": [
459: "SOURCE_RESOURCE_NAME_1",
460: "SOURCE_RESOURCE_NAME_2"
461: ]
462: }'
463: Replace the following:
464: ENDPOINT_LOCATION: the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following
465: values:
466: us for the US multi-region
467: eu for the EU multi-region
468: global for the Global location
469: For more information, see
470: Specify a multi-region
471: for your data store.
472: PROJECT_NUMBER: the number of your Google Cloud project.
473: LOCATION:
474: the geographic location of your data store, such as global.
475: For more information, see Locations.
476: NOTEBOOK_ID: The unique identifier of the notebook.
477: SOURCE_RESOURCE_NAME: the complete resource name
478: of the data source to be deleted. This field has the pattern:
479: projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks/NOTEBOOK_ID/source/SOURCE_ID.
480: If the request is successful, you should receive an empty JSON object.

139: Save and categorize content based on your preferences.
140: This page describes the start-up tasks that you must complete to set up
141: Gemini Notebook for business.
142: After you have performed the tasks on this page, your users can
143: start creating and using notebooks in Gemini Notebook for business.
144: About identity setup
145: To complete the setup, you must have your organization's identity provider (IdP)
146: configured in Google Cloud.
147: Correct setup for identity is important for two reasons:
148: It lets your users use their current corporate credentials to access the
149: Gemini Notebook for business user interface.
150: It ensures that users see only the notebooks which they own or which have
151: been shared with them.
152: Supported frameworks
153: The following authentication frameworks are supported:
154: Cloud Identity:
155: Case 1: If you use Cloud Identity or Google Workspace, then all
156: user identities and user groups are present and managed through
157: Google Cloud. For more information about Cloud Identity, see the
158: Cloud Identity documentation.
159: Case 2: You use a third-party IdP, and you have synced
160: identities with Cloud Identity. Your end users use
161: Cloud Identity to
162: authenticate before accessing Google resources or Google Workspace.
163: Case 3: You use a third-party IdP, and you have synced
164: identities with Cloud Identity. However, you are still using your
165: existing third-party IdP to perform the authentication. You
166: have configured SSO with Cloud Identity such that your users begin
167: their sign in using Cloud Identity and then get directed to your
168: third-party IdP. (You might have already done this sync when
169: setting up other Google Cloud resources or Google Workspace.)
170: Workforce Identity Federation: If you use an external identity
171: provider (Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Ping, PingFederate, or
172: another OIDC or SAML 2.0 IdP), but don't want to sync your
173: identities into Cloud Identity, then you must set up
174: Workforce Identity Federation in Google Cloud
175: before you can turn on data source access control for Gemini Notebook for business.
176: The google.subject attribute must map to the email address field in the
177: external IdP. The following are example google.subject and
178: google.groups attribute mappings for commonly used IdPs:
179: Microsoft Entra ID
180: Microsoft Entra ID with OIDC protocol
181: google.subject=assertion.email.lowerAscii()
182: google.groups=assertion.groups
183: Microsoft Entra ID with SAML protocol
184: google.subject=assertion.attributes['http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/ws/2005/05/identity/claims/name'][0].lowerAscii()
185: google.groups=assertion.attributes['http://schemas.microsoft.com/ws/2008/06/identity/claims/groups']
186: Microsoft Entra ID with a large number of groups
187: If you use Microsoft Entra ID and have more than approximately 150
188: groups, then you should follow the setup procedures for a large number
189: of groups.
190: google.subject=user.emails[0].value.lowerAscii()
191: google.groups=group.externalId
192: Note: If you use System for Cross-domain Identity Management
193: (SCIM) (or extended
194: attributes), the google.groups attribute mapping is ignored.
195: Okta
196: Okta with OIDC protocol
197: google.subject=assertion.email.lowerAscii()
198: google.groups=assertion.groups
199: Okta with SAML protocol
200: google.subject=assertion.subject.lowerAscii()
201: google.groups=assertion.attributes['groups']
202: You can select only one IdP per Google Cloud project.
203: Before you begin
204: Before starting the procedures on this page, make sure that one of the following
205: is true:
206: You use Cloud Identity as your IdP, or
207: You use a third-party IdP and have configured SSO with
208: Cloud Identity, or
209: You use a third-party IdP that is not Okta and have:
210: Set up Workforce Identity Federation by following the instructions
211: in
212: Configure Workforce Identity Federation with Microsoft Entra ID and sign in users or, if you have
213: more than approximately 150 groups, in Configure Workforce Identity Federation
214: with Microsoft Entra ID with a large number of groups.
215: If you follow the
216: Configure Workforce Identity Federation with Microsoft Entra ID and sign in users instructions,
217: make sure to do the recommended
218: security best practice steps to add a group
219: claim
220: and select All groups. This is a required step for
221: Gemini Notebook for business.
222: Set up SCIM. See Configure SCIM in Microsoft Entra
223: ID.
224: SCIM is necessary for autocomplete of user emails and group
225: names
226: and for Microsoft Entra ID with
227: a large number of groups.
228: You use Okta as your third-party IdP and have:
229: Followed the instructions in
230: Configure Workforce Identity Federation with
231: Okta.
232: Set up SCIM. See Configure SCIM in Okta.
233: SCIM is necessary for
234: autocomplete of user emails and group
235: names.
236: Plan your Workforce Identity Federation configuration
237: If you use Workforce Identity Federation, do the following before your users start
238: creating notebooks:
239: Map google.subject by using .lowerAscii() in the attribute mapping of
240: your workforce identity pool provider, as shown in the examples in
241: Supported frameworks.
242: Gemini Notebook for business matches user identities exactly.
243: If your IdP asserts a user's email address with uppercase letters in one
244: sign-in and lowercase letters in another, the user is treated as two
245: different users. Sharing a notebook with a manually entered email address
246: also works only when the address matches the asserted identity exactly.
247: Don't change the google.subject mapping after your users have started
248: creating notebooks. The mapping is part of each user's identity. If you
249: change it, existing notebooks, licenses, and shares no longer match the
250: users who own them.
251: Set the session duration of the workforce identity pool to cover your
252: users' workday. You can set a duration of up to 12 hours by using the
253: --session-duration flag of the gcloud iam workforce-pools update
254: command. The default session duration is one hour.
255: Federated sign-in sessions can't be refreshed silently. When the pool
256: session expires, users are redirected to the sign-in page and lose unsaved
257: chat conversations. For more information, see
258: Update a pool.
259: Create a project and enable the API
260: If you already have a Google Cloud project that you want to use, start at step
261: 2.
262: Sign in to your Google Cloud account. If you're new to
263: Google Cloud,
264: create an account to evaluate how our products perform in
265: real-world scenarios. New customers also get $300 in free credits to
266: run, test, and deploy workloads.
267: In the Google Cloud console, on the project selector page,
268: select or create a Google Cloud project.
269: Roles required to select or create a project
270: Select a project: Selecting a project doesn't require a specific
271: IAM role—you can select any project that you've been
272: granted a role on.
273: Create a project: To create a project, you need the Project Creator role
274: (roles/resourcemanager.projectCreator), which contains the
275: resourcemanager.projects.create permission. Learn how to grant
276: roles.
277: Note: If you don't plan to keep the
278: resources that you create in this procedure, create a project instead of
279: selecting an existing project. After you finish these steps, you can
280: delete the project, removing all resources associated with the project.
281: Go to project selector
282: Verify that billing is enabled for your Google Cloud project.
283: Enable the Discovery Engine API, if it is not already enabled.
284: Roles required to enable APIs
285: To enable APIs, you need the serviceusage.services.enable permission. If you
286: created the project, then you likely already have this permission through the
287: Owner role (roles/owner). Otherwise, you can get this permission through the
288: Service Usage Admin role (roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin).
289: Learn how to grant roles.
290: Enable the API
291: In the Google Cloud console, on the project selector page,
292: select or create a Google Cloud project.
293: Roles required to select or create a project
294: Select a project: Selecting a project doesn't require a specific
295: IAM role—you can select any project that you've been
296: granted a role on.
297: Create a project: To create a project, you need the Project Creator role
298: (roles/resourcemanager.projectCreator), which contains the
299: resourcemanager.projects.create permission. Learn how to grant
300: roles.
301: Note: If you don't plan to keep the
302: resources that you create in this procedure, create a project instead of
303: selecting an existing project. After you finish these steps, you can
304: delete the project, removing all resources associated with the project.
305: Go to project selector
306: Verify that billing is enabled for your Google Cloud project.
307: Enable the Discovery Engine API, if it is not already enabled.
308: Roles required to enable APIs
309: To enable APIs, you need the serviceusage.services.enable permission. If you
310: created the project, then you likely already have this permission through the
311: Owner role (roles/owner). Otherwise, you can get this permission through the
312: Service Usage Admin role (roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin).
313: Learn how to grant roles.
314: Enable the API
315: Grant the Cloud NotebookLM Admin role
316: As the project owner, you need to assign the Cloud NotebookLM Admin role to any
317: users who you want to be able to administer Gemini Notebook for business in this project:
318: In the Google Cloud console, go to the IAM page.
319: Go to IAM
320: Select the project.
321: Click person_add Grant access.
322: In the New principals field, enter the user identifier.
323: This is typically the email address for a Google Account or a user
324: group.
325: In the Select a role list, select Cloud NotebookLM Admin.
326: For more information, see
327: User
328: roles.
329: Click Save.
330: Set the IdP for Gemini Notebook for business
331: The project owner or a user who has the Cloud NotebookLM Admin role can set up
332: the IdP.
333: In the Google Cloud console, go to the Gemini Notebook for business
334: page.
335: Gemini Enterprise
336: Set Identity settings to Google identity provider or
337: Third-party identity provider.
338: For more information, see About identity setup above.
339: If you are using a third-party IdP and
340: Workforce Identity Federation, then specify the name of your
341: workforce pool and your Workforce pool provider.
342: Copy the Link.
343: You will send out this link to all the end-users of
344: Gemini Notebook for business. This
345: is the link to the user interface that they'll use to create, edit, and share
346: notebooks.
347: Optional: Register customer-managed encryption keys
348: If you want to use customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) instead of Google
349: default encryption, then follow the instructions to register a key for
350: Gemini Notebook for business in Customer-managed encryption keys.
351: Typically, you only need to use CMEK if your organization has strict regulatory
352: requirements or internal policies that stipulate control over encryption keys.
353: In most situations, Google default encryption is sufficient. For general
354: information about CMEK, see the Cloud Key Management Service documentation.
355: Important: Register your key before your users start creating notebooks.
356: Any notebooks created before the CMEK encryption is set up, won't be protected.
357: Grant Gemini Notebook for business roles to users
358: This section describes how to give your users the IAM roles that
359: they need to access, manage, and share notebooks.
360: In the Google Cloud console, go to the IAM page.
361: Go to IAM
362: Select the project.
363: Click person_add Grant access.
364: In the New principals field, enter the user identifier. This is
365: typically the email address for a Google Account, a user group or the
366: identifier for a user in a workforce identity pool. For details, see
367: Represent workforce pool users in IAM policies, or
368: contact your administrator.
369: In the Select a role list, select Cloud NotebookLM User
370: role.
371: Click Save.
372: In addition to the Cloud NotebookLM User role, users need a license for
373: Gemini Notebook for business. See Get licenses for
374: Gemini Notebook for business.
375: Note: The subscription page displays the previous name NotebookLM Enterprise.
376: What's next

140: This page describes how to get subscriptions for Gemini Notebook Enterprise,
141: assign licenses to your users, and what to do when subscriptions expire.
142: Note: NotebookLM Enterprise is renamed to
143: Gemini Notebook Enterprise, but the subscription name remains
144: NotebookLM Enterprise.
145: About licenses
146: To sign in to the Gemini Notebook Enterprise app, a user must have
147: a license. Licenses can be assigned to users manually or automatically.
148: Manually-assigned licenses: These belong to an individual user and are
149: associated with the user's email address.
150: Manually-assigned licenses are best for users who rely on the
151: Gemini Notebook Enterprise app and use it often.
152: Automatically-assigned licenses: You can choose to have licenses that are
153: part of a subscription be automatically assigned to a user the first time
154: that the user accesses the Gemini Notebook Enterprise interface.
155: This is a way to distribute licenses in bulk without having to assign licenses
156: to each individual separately.
157: Licenses are specific to multi-region. For example, if users want access to
158: notebooks in both the us multi-region and global, assign them a license in
159: each.
160: About subscriptions
161: You buy licenses by the subscription. A subscription contains at least 15
162: licenses and can contain up to 5,000 licenses. If you need more than 5,000
163: licenses, contact your Google sales representative.
164: Subscriptions are specific to multi-regions. Users who create notebooks
165: in the global region need licenses from a global subscription. Similarly,
166: users who need to keep their notebooks and data in the European Union need
167: licenses from an eu subscription.
168: There are two subscription tiers for Gemini Notebook Enterprise:
169: The free-trial tier: With this tier, you get a full-featured, 14-day trial
170: subscription of 5000 licenses.
171: The paid tier: You can buy a monthly subscription or a year-long
172: subscription. Both the monthly and the yearly subscriptions can be set to renew
173: automatically.
174: Before you begin
175: Before starting the procedures on this page, make sure that:
176: You have completed the tasks on the
177: Set up Gemini Notebook Enterprise. This includes granting
178: at least the Cloud NotebookLM User (roles/discoveryengine.notebookLmUser)
179: role to any users who you'll license to use
180: Gemini Notebook Enterprise (including free-trial users).
181: You have the following roles:
182: Cloud NotebookLM Admin (roles/discoveryengine.notebookLmOwner)
183: Gemini Enterprise Admin (roles/discoveryengine.agentspaceAdmin)
184: Get a subscription
185: A paid subscription is billed to the Cloud Billing account that's linked to
186: your project when you add the subscription. You don't choose a billing account
187: on the Add subscription page. For more information about switching billing
188: accounts, see Switch to a different billing
189: account.
190: To get a subscription for Gemini Notebook Enterprise, do the
191: following:
192: Optional: To have the subscription billed to a different billing account,
193: link your project to that billing account. For more information, see
194: Change the Cloud Billing account linked to a
195: project.
196: This change also moves the project's other Google Cloud charges to that
197: billing account.
198: In the Google Cloud console, go to the Gemini Enterprise page.
199: Gemini Enterprise
200: Click Manage users.
201: Choose a Multi-region for your subscription. If you don't have
202: compliance or regulatory reasons to locate your data in the US or EU
203: multi-regions, Google recommends that you choose the global region for
204: maximum availability and low latency.
205: Click add Add
206: subscription.
207: On the Add subscription page:
208: Enter the Number of licenses that you want.
209: Choose the Term for the subscription.
210: Optional: Click Auto renew.
211: Select your tier.
212: Click Add.
213: Switch to a different billing account
214: You might need to bill your Gemini Notebook Enterprise licenses
215: to a different Cloud Billing account, for example, if your
216: organization moves to a new one. The Edit subscription page doesn't let
217: you change a subscription's billing account. Instead, you create a new
218: subscription that's billed to the new billing account and transfer your users
219: to it.
220: To switch billing accounts, follow these steps:
221: If auto renew is on for the existing subscription, turn it off:
222: In the Google Cloud console, go to the Gemini Enterprise page.
223: Gemini Enterprise
224: Click Manage users.
225: Select the Multi-region of the existing subscription.
226: Click Edit for the subscription, clear Auto renew, and then
227: click Save. If Edit isn't available for the subscription,
228: contact your Google sales representative.
229: Link your project to the new billing account. For more information, see
230: Change the Cloud Billing account linked to a
231: project.
232: This change also moves the project's other Google Cloud charges to the
233: new billing account.
234: Get a subscription in the same multi-region. The new
235: subscription is billed to the new billing account, starting as soon as you
236: add it. Your existing subscription is typically still billed to the old
237: billing account until its term ends.
238: Important: To avoid paying for overlapping subscriptions, add the new
239: subscription shortly before the existing one expires. If the existing
240: subscription expires before you add the new one, users can't sign in until
241: you transfer them to the new subscription.
242: Transfer your users to the new subscription, either
243: manually or automatically when the existing
244: subscription expires.
245: Add users and manually assign them licenses
246: To manually assign licenses to users from a subscription, do the following:
247: In the Google Cloud console, go to the Gemini Enterprise page.
248: Gemini Enterprise
249: Click Manage users.
250: Select the Multi-region of the existing license.
251: Click Add users.
252: On the Add users page:
253: Enter the email addresses of the users. Make sure to use the same email
254: address that they'll use to sign in to the
255: Gemini Notebook Enterprise app.
256: Select the subscription to assign to those users.
257: Click Submit.
258: Add users and assign them licenses automatically
259: To assign licenses to users automatically when they sign in to the
260: Gemini Notebook Enterprise app, do the following:
261: In the Google Cloud console, go to the Gemini Enterprise page.
262: Gemini Enterprise
263: Click Manage users.
264: Select the Multi-region of the existing license.
265: Make sure that you have a subscription with enough licenses for
266: the maximum number of users that you expect be signed in to
267: Gemini Notebook Enterprise at any one time.
268: Select Assign licenses automatically and then select the subscription.
269: A license from this subscription is assigned each time a user who doesn't
270: have a manually-assigned license signs in.
271: If no licenses remain in the subscription, users are shown a message
272: notifying them that they don't have access.
273: Transfer licenses from expired subscriptions
274: Users can't sign in to Gemini Notebook Enterprise if the subscription
275: has expired. There are a couple of approaches to returning sign-in access to
276: them:
277: Automatically transfer users with expired licenses to the default
278: subscription.
279: Manually transfer users to a new subscription.
280: Automatically transfer users to an active subscription
281: To automatically transfer users to an active subscription, do the following:
282: In the Google Cloud console, go to the Gemini Enterprise page.
283: Gemini Enterprise
284: Click Manage users.
285: Select the Multi-region of the existing license.
286: Make sure that you have an active subscription. If you don't have one, get
287: a subscription.
288: Select Assign licenses automatically and choose the active subscription.
289: Select Automatically update expired license.
290: When a user with an expired license next signs in, they are automatically
291: granted a license in the chosen subscription.
292: Manually transfer users to an active subscription
293: To manually transfer users to an active subscription, do the following:
294: In the Google Cloud console, go to the Gemini Enterprise page.
295: Gemini Enterprise
296: Click Manage users.
297: Select the Multi-region of the existing license.
298: Make sure that you have an active subscription. If you don't have one, get
299: a subscription.
300: Select the users and click Assign different license.
301: In the Edit Users pane, select the subscription and click Submit.
302: What's next
303: Share the sign-in link for Gemini Notebook Enterprise with your users.
304: See step 5 of Set the identity provider for
305: Gemini Notebook Enterprise.
306: If your users need instructions on how to share notebooks or revoke sharing
307: on notebooks, see Share notebooks. Sharing is one feature
308: of Gemini Notebook that is different between the personal Gemini Notebook product and
309: Gemini Notebook Enterprise.
310: If your users need guidance on how to use Gemini Notebook, see
311: the user documentation for
312: Gemini Notebook. Note that there are some
313: differences between Gemini Notebook and Gemini Notebook Enterprise. See
314: What is Gemini Notebook Enterprise.
315: Send feedback

155: NotebookLM MCP Server
156: An MCP server for NotebookLM (notebooklm.google.com).
157: Note: Tested with Pro/free tier accounts. May work with NotebookLM Enterprise accounts but has not been tested.
158: 📺 Watch the Demos

220: Important Disclaimer
221: This MCP uses internal APIs that:
222: Are undocumented and may change without notice
223: Require cookie extraction from your browser (I have a tool for that!)
224: Use at your own risk for personal/experimental purposes.
225: Installation
226: Install from PyPI using your preferred Python package manager:
227: Using uv (Recommended)
228: uv tool install notebooklm-mcp-server
229: Using pip
230: pip install notebooklm-mcp-server
231: Using pipx
232: pipx install notebooklm-mcp-server
233: Alternative: Install from Source
234: # Clone the repository
235: git clone https://github.com/jacob-bd/notebooklm-mcp.git
236: cd notebooklm-mcp
237: # Install with uv
238: uv tool install .
239: Upgrading
240: # Using uv
241: uv tool upgrade notebooklm-mcp-server
242: # Using pip
243: pip install --upgrade notebooklm-mcp-server
244: # Using pipx
245: pipx upgrade notebooklm-mcp-server
246: After upgrading, restart your AI tool to reconnect to the updated MCP server:
247: Claude Code: Restart the application, or use /mcp to reconnect
248: Cursor: Restart the application
249: Gemini CLI: Restart the CLI session
250: Uninstalling
251: To completely remove the MCP:
252: # Using uv
253: uv tool uninstall notebooklm-mcp-server
254: # Using pip
255: pip uninstall notebooklm-mcp-server
256: # Using pipx
257: pipx uninstall notebooklm-mcp-server
258: # Remove cached auth tokens (optional)
259: rm -rf ~/.notebooklm-mcp
260: Also remove from your AI tools:
261: Tool
262: Command
263: Claude Code
264: claude mcp remove notebooklm-mcp
265: Gemini CLI
266: gemini mcp remove notebooklm-mcp
267: Cursor/VS Code
268: Remove entry from ~/.cursor/mcp.json or ~/.vscode/mcp.json
269: Authentication
270: Before using the MCP, you need to authenticate with NotebookLM. Run:
271: # Recommended: Auto mode (launches Chrome, you log in)
272: notebooklm-mcp-auth
273: # Alternative: File mode (manual cookie extraction)
274: notebooklm-mcp-auth --file
275: Auto mode launches a dedicated Chrome profile, you log in to Google, and cookies are extracted automatically. Your login persists for future auth refreshes.
276: File mode shows instructions for manually extracting cookies from Chrome DevTools and saving them to a file.
277: After successful auth, add the MCP to your AI tool and restart.
278: For detailed instructions, troubleshooting, and how the authentication system works, see docs/AUTHENTICATION.md.
279: MCP Configuration
280: ⚠️ Context Window Warning: This MCP provides 31 tools which consume a significant portion of your context window. It's recommended to disable the MCP when not actively using NotebookLM to preserve context for your other work. In Claude Code, use @notebooklm-mcp to toggle it on/off, or use /mcp command.

316: HTTP Support (Open WebUI)

319: See docs/MULTI_USER_ANALYSIS.md for detailed multi-user deployment guides.
320: Claude Code (Recommended CLI Method)

423: Authentication Lifecycle
424: Component
425: Duration
426: Refresh
427: Cookies
428: ~2-4 weeks
429: Auto-refresh via headless Chrome (if profile saved)
430: CSRF Token
431: ~minutes
432: Auto-refreshed on every request failure
433: Session ID
434: Per MCP session

436: v0.1.9+: The server now automatically handles token expiration:
437: Refreshes CSRF tokens immediately when expired
438: Reloads cookies from disk if updated externally
439: Runs headless Chrome auth if profile has saved login
440: You can also call refresh_auth() to explicitly reload tokens.
441: If automatic refresh fails (Google login fully expired), run notebooklm-mcp-auth again.
442: Troubleshooting
443: uv tool upgrade Not Installing Latest Version
444: Symptoms:
445: Running uv tool upgrade notebooklm-mcp-server installs an older version (e.g., 0.1.5 instead of 0.1.9)
446: uv cache clean doesn't fix the issue
447: Why this happens: uv tool upgrade respects version constraints from your original installation. If you initially installed an older version or with a constraint, upgrade stays within those bounds by design.
448: Fix — Force reinstall:
449: uv tool install --force notebooklm-mcp-server
450: This bypasses any cached constraints and installs the absolute latest version from PyPI.
451: Verify:
452: uv tool list | grep notebooklm
453: # Should show: notebooklm-mcp-server v0.1.9 (or latest)
454: Chrome DevTools MCP Not Working (Cursor/Gemini CLI)
455: If Chrome DevTools MCP shows "no tools, prompts or resources" or fails to start, it's likely due to a known npx bug with the puppeteer-core module.
456: Symptoms:
457: Cursor/Gemini CLI shows MCP as connected but with "No tools, prompts, or resources"
458: Process spawn errors in logs: spawn pnpx ENOENT or module not found errors
459: Can't extract cookies for NotebookLM authentication
460: Fix:
461: Install pnpm (if not already installed):
462: npm install -g pnpm
463: Update Chrome DevTools MCP configuration:
464: For Cursor (~/.cursor/mcp.json):
465: "chrome-devtools": {
466: "command": "pnpm",
467: "args": ["dlx", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest", "--browser-url=http://127.0.0.1:9222"]
468: }
469: For Gemini CLI (~/.gemini/settings.json):
470: "chrome-devtools": {
471: "command": "pnpm",
472: "args": ["dlx", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest"]
473: }
474: Restart your IDE/CLI for changes to take effect.
475: Why this happens: Chrome DevTools MCP uses puppeteer-core which changed its module path in v23+, but npx caching behavior causes module resolution failures. Using pnpm dlx avoids this issue.
476: Related Issues:
477: ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp#160
478: ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp#111
479: ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp#221
480: Limitations
481: Rate limits: Free tier has ~50 queries/day
482: No official support: API may change without notice
483: Cookie expiration: Need to re-extract cookies every few weeks
484: Contributing
485: See CLAUDE.md for detailed API documentation and how to add new features.
486: Vibe Coding Alert
487: Full transparency: this project was built by a non-developer using AI coding assistants. If you're an experienced Python developer, you might look at this codebase and wince. That's okay.
488: The goal here was to scratch an itch - programmatic access to NotebookLM - and learn along the way. The code works, but it's likely missing patterns, optimizations, or elegance that only years of experience can provide.
489: This is where you come in. If you see something that makes you cringe, please consider contributing rather than just closing the tab. This is open source specifically because human expertise is irreplaceable. Whether it's refactoring, better error handling, type hints, or architectural guidance - PRs and issues are welcome.
490: Think of it as a chance to mentor an AI-assisted developer through code review. We all benefit when experienced developers share their knowledge.
491: Credits

271: We strongly recommend using the official client libraries, which are implemented using gRPC except for the Perl library.
272: The Google Ads API supports calls via either gRPC or REST interfaces, both utilizing a resource-oriented design.
273: Official client libraries are recommended for their idiomatic, type-safe code and handling of low-level communication details.
274: This guide specifically details how to call the REST interface directly without using a Google-supported client library.
275: Key Point: We strongly recommend using our official client
276: libraries wherever you can. All Google provided client
277: libraries are implemented using gRPC, except for the Perl
278: library, which uses the REST
279: interface. Unless you are specifically looking for details about REST, consult
280: the reference documentation for details that cover both our
281: official client libraries and the REST transport layer.Note: If you are new to the Google Ads API, we recommend reading the Getting
282: Started guide first, which covers how to
283: set up your account and make your first API call. Make sure to follow the curl
284: tab.
285: The Google Ads API can be called either using gRPC or REST. Both
286: interfaces expose a resource-oriented design
287: shared with other Google Cloud APIs.
288: We recommend using Google's official client libraries
289: wherever possible. They provide idiomatic, type-safe code in each supported
290: language and handle many low-level details of communication with the API (like
291: timeout settings, result set pagination, and
292: authentication). Our client libraries also include an
293: extensive set of code examples and utilities that assist with
294: common tasks, such as constructing
295: resource names and handling
296: field masks.
297: This guide presents details specific to REST and explains what you need to know
298: to call the REST interface directly, without the use of a Google-supported
299: client library. This guide may be useful if you are writing your own custom code
300: to use REST directly or using a third-party HTTP client library.

32: This is an officially supported package, maintained by a member of the Sherlock Project itself.
33: pipx is often recommended over pip, having more predictable behavior.
34: pipx install sherlock-project
35: For those who prefer classic pip, it’s very similar. Userspace is recommended.
36: pip install --user sherlock-project
37: That’s it! You can now run sherlock from anywhere.
38: sherlock --version
39: This package is not officially supported, but it’s maintained by a trusted packager.
40: brew install sherlock
41: That’s it! You can now run sherlock from anywhere.
42: sherlock --version
43: This package is not officially supported, but it’s maintained under the trusted purview of the Debian Security Tools Packaging Team. The ParrotOS image is maintained by the ParrotOS team.We may begin to officially support this package in the future.
44: Supported distributions are Kali and ParrotOS. Work is underway to support Debian, Ubuntu, and others.
45: sudo apt install sherlock
46: That’s it! You can now run sherlock from anywhere.
47: sherlock --version
48: This is an officially supported package, maintained by a member of the Sherlock Project itself.Sherlock has out-of-the-box support for Fedora. Enterprise Linux support through EPEL is planned.
49: Enterprise Linux distributions are RHEL, CentOS, Alma, Rocky, Oracle, and Scientific.
50: sudo dnf install sherlock-project
51: That’s it! You can now run sherlock from anywhere.
52: sherlock --version
53: This package is not officially supported, but still closely follows our release cycle.
54: sudo pacman -S sherlock
55: That’s it! You can now run sherlock from anywhere.
56: sherlock --version
57: This is an officially supported image, maintained by a member of the Sherlock Project itself.
58: docker pull sherlock/sherlock
59: Sherlock doesn’t yet have context detection. It’s recommended that Docker containers be ran with option -o /opt/sherlock/results/{user123}.txt (replace {user123}) when an output file is desired at the mounted volume (as seen in the compose). This has no effect on stdout, which functions as expected out of the box.
60: # One-off searches
61: docker run --rm -t sherlock/sherlock user123
62: # If you need to save the output file... (modify as needed)
63: # Output file will land in ${pwd}/results
64: docker run --rm -t -v "$PWD/results:/opt/sherlock/results" sherlock/sherlock -o /opt/sherlock/results/text.txt user123
65: # At any time, you may update the image via this command
66: docker pull sherlock/sherlock
67: Using compose
68: version: "3"
69: services:
70: sherlock:
71: container_name: sherlock
72: image: sherlock/sherlock
73: volumes:
74: - ./sherlock/:/opt/sherlock/results/
75: docker compose run sherlock user123
76: Build image from source (useful for contributors)
77: # Assumes ${pwd} is repository root
78: docker build -t sherlock .
79: docker run --rm -t sherlock user123
80: While this method uses the official repository, it’s not an officially supported installation method. This method is recommended for contributors, packagers, and other users who need access to the source code.
81: git clone https://github.com/sherlock-project/sherlock.git
82: cd sherlock
83: virtualenv .
84: source bin/activate
85: Build live package from source (useful for contributors)
86: Building an editable (or live) package links the entry point to your current directory, rather than to the standard install location. This is often useful when working with the code base, as changes are reflected immediately without reinstallation.Note that the version number will be 0.0.0 for pipx local builds unless manually changed in the pyproject file (it will prompt the user for an update).
87: pipx install -e .
88: Run package from source (without installing)
89: If you’d rather not install directly to your system, you can import the module at runtime with -m.
90: python3 -m sherlock_project user123 user789

evidence.observation: quote: What is the HubSpot Developer Platform?

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: The HubSpot Developer Platform is a unified foundation that empowers you to build and deliver value faster — one way to build on HubSpot, from private integrations to Marketplace apps. It includes the CLI, projects framework, UI extensions, and APIs plus an AI‑ready framework and capabilities like Breeze Agent Tools.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Projects are the unified framework for building apps (and CMS assets) on the HubSpot Developer Platform: unified projects that can support one account or many. A project is a collection of code, configuration, and assets managed through the CLI with date-based versioning (like 2026.03).

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: When are new platform versions and APIs released?

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Both follow the same 6-month release cycle: March and September. Each platform version is supported for 18 months, giving you ample time to plan upgrades. API versioning is independent meaning you can use newer APIs on older platform versions.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: There are two authentication types available based on how you plan to distribute your app: OAuth is required for multiple accounts, while static auth access tokens are used for installing in a single account at a time.

evidence.observation: quote: OAuth

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: If you plan to distribute your app to multiple accounts (either through listing on the HubSpot Marketplace or by managing specific authorized accounts), your app must be built using OAuth authentication. You’ll need to set up and host an OAuth backend service (e.g., hosted as a Docker instance using a cloud service provider) to initiate the OAuth process and manage token data for users installing your app in their account.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: HubSpot provides a Node.js quickstart guide here, which includes code you can run in a Docker instance with full OAuth support. Authentication configuration details for your app are available on the app details page in the developer overview of your HubSpot account.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Once you’ve set up an OAuth backend, you can make API requests using the OAuth access token that corresponds to a user who installed your app. This access token is provided using the Bearer HTTP authorization header. For example, if you wanted to retrieve contacts for the account with an access token of 00000000-aaaa-xxx-yyyy-zzzzzzzzzzzz, your request would resemble the following:
